speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to be permitted to say a few words on a question of privilege raised in my absence from the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). Yesterday afternoon I returned from the United Nations in order to come before the house to answer some of the questions which were asked here last Tuesday afternoon. On Tuesday night I sent the Minister of Transport a wire from our Canadian mission in New York, which reads as follows:
Winnipeg Tribune reporter called me at 2.30 p.m. local time today asking me what I had meant in the story of our annual meeting in Winnipeg South at Lois Parkhill November 5, when I said "Mr. Mcllraith showed me the Dixon-Speas report."
I explained that I had made a courtesy call on you while in Ottawa when attending the federal Liberal women's conference. At that time you stated the Dixon-Speas report could not be released and pointed to four volumes on the table behind your desk. The reporter asked me if I had been talking to Ottawa today, to which I said no. He told me of Mr. Orlikow's statement in the house.
Now, there are two points I would like to make. Because of my deep concern over the problem of T.C.A., this summer I went through the overhaul base and visited with the men. On another occasion I met with management. I was shown reports, records and documents, so that when I saw the Dixon-Speas report on the minister's table I well understood this report would probably contain confidential information. At the annual meeting of the Winnipeg South constituency, when reporting on the T.C.A. question I did say, without giving any details, that the Minister of Transport had shown me the Dixon-Speas report. It was unthinking of me to allow any impression that I had seen the report itself.
On reviewing the newspaper stories of our meeting I realized how I must have embarrassed both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport. For this reason, on Tuesday night I telephoned the chairman of my advisory committee in Winnipeg to ask him if at any time I had given any suggestion that I had read the Dixon-Speas report. As 28902-5-301J
a result the following wire was sent to the Minister of Transport from the Winnipeg South Liberal association and a copy was sent to me in New York yesterday morning:
Mrs. Konantz did not say at her annual meeting or elsewhere that she had seen and therefore read the Dixon-Speas report but did say that the five volume report was pointed out to her by the minister. From her conversation with him she could well understand why the information contained in it could not be made public because it would then be available to the competitors of T.C.A.
Yesterday morning the Minister of Transport wired me to come to Ottawa. I have now had a chance to read the questions which were raised in the house on Tuesday. I believe I have given frank answers to them all. I have read the statement made by the Minister of Transport to the House of Commons. Needless to say, it is entirely correct.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEBATES-CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXPANSION OF ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I should like to make an announcement on a subject which I am sure will be of considerable interest to the house and to the Canadian people. I refer to Canada's program of economic assistance for the developing nations of the world. The record demonstrates, I think, that since 1950, when Canada was one of the founding members of the Colombo plan, Canadian governments have regularly reviewed the adequacy of their aid programs and have made provision for increases whenever national circumstances permitted. Last year only was a reduction

Expansion of Economic Assistance made in the level of our assistance as part of a general program to reduce expenditures in every area of government activities.
When the present government took office it became increasingly apparent that because of the changing framework of international assistance a fresh look was required at our international aid effort. The requirements of the developing countries are urgent and growing, and economic assistance for them has become an established policy of all of the advanced nations of the free world which have recognized the need to co-operate in assisting to the best of their ability those countries in the process of economic development.
Accordingly, our Canadian aid effort cannot be viewed in isolation but rather as part of a broad collective effort. We would be failing in our responsibilities both to the developing countries and to other advanced countries with which we are associated, if we did not ensure that Canada played its proper role in this common aid effort.
As an integral part of our foreign policy our Canadian aid programs have, I am convinced, the broad support of the Canadian people. By sharing our resources, skills and experiences we not only benefit others but also help to expand and enrich our own experiences. Our aid programs provide a stimulus to the domestic economy and contribute to a betterment of employment conditions, since the main part of our aid funds is spent in Canada to purchase Canadian goods and services required in the developing countries.
Taking all these factors into account, the Canadian government has now formulated general plans for an expansion of Canada's aid programs beginning in the fiscal year 1964-65.
The main proposed area of expansion would be in special Canadian lending for development purposes. If Canada is to be in a position to provide assistance on terms commensurate with the needs of recipient countries, consistent with the agreed objectives of international bodies of which we are a member, and in line with what other major donors are providing, there should be available for implementing Canada's bilateral assistance programs facilities for lending of the type now carried out by the international development association, involving such features as long maturity periods, liberal grace periods, and little or no interest. It is proposed, therefore, that a lending program of this type should be commenced in the fiscal year 1964-65 with an initial ceiling for commitments of $50 million.
It is the government's intention to ask parliament to make separate provision beginning

in 1964-65 for a food aid program, as already announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and for Canada's contribution to the Indus basin development fund, which was set up in an effort to resolve the difficult dispute between India and Pakistan over the use of the waters of the Indus basin. These are now included in Canada's bilateral grant aid programs, which will be continued in 1964-65 at their present level of about $50 million, but which will in the future be limited to the provision of project assistance, the supply of industrial commodities and the carrying out of technical assistance for the developing countries. The result will be a significant increase in our grant aid.
These improvements in our aid programs would, of course, be additional to Canada's other existing programs of assistance, including our long term financing arrangements under the Export Credits Insurance Act and our contributions to the multilateral programs of the United Nations. Recent references have been made in the house to the increased Canadian contribution to the United Nations special fund and the international development association.
In the current fiscal year it is expected that the over-all level of Canada's expenditures for assistance to less developed countries will be in the neighbourhood of $120 million. It is the government's intention to seek authority to make available an additional $70 million in 1964-65. It is, of course, not possible at this stage to forecast an actual expenditure level for 1964-65, but it is expected that with the new resources available, the level might be in the range of $180 million to $190 million.
The over-all program which I have described will be a flexible one designed to place Canada in a position to make an effective response to changing national and international circumstances. In particular, it will provide:
(1)	aid to Colombo plan countries of Asia at a higher level than was provided prior to the reduction in 1962;
(2)	a more comprehensive and sizeable Canadian program for the commonwealth countries of the Caribbean. In this connection, it will be remembered that when the Prime Minister of Canada saw the President of the United States he indicated that it was Canada's intention to increase its assistance to the commonwealth countries of the Caribbean with which Canada, of course, has a long and historic association;
(3)	a larger and more effective program for Africa, including the French speaking states;
(4)	a further contribution to Latin American development, in close co-operation with the

inter-American development bank, through the availability of new and additional lending resources.
I make this announcement at this time in view of the O.E.C.D. ministerial meeting in Paris next Tuesday and Wednesday, at which the subject of aid to developing countries will be discussed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DEBATES-CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXPANSION OF ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
It is difficult, Mr. Speaker, to follow the minister in the detail in which he indulged without having before one the actual figures and the computations that he has before him as he speaks. However, in so far as a program is concerned which will raise standards in other parts of the world and will assure technical assistance, in what the minister has stated he represents the viewpoint of the Canadian people.
As a matter of fact, when we came into office we made alterations in the amount of assistance given under the Colombo plan by increasing the amount from $35 million to approximately $50 million. Furthermore, during our period of office we brought into effect assistance for those developing French speaking countries in Africa, a work which was particularly appreciated by those people in view of the dual nature of our country. Mention is made in the announcement of expanding assistance to the Caribbean countries. This is a continuation of a course which we launched in 1959. It is a worthy one, for those nations have much in common with us, and contiguous to us as they are within the commonwealth they have a particular claim upon our consideration.
In so far as the loan plan is concerned, that is something that will have to be examined with care. I believe that Canada, as a member of the commonwealth, should do her part toward encouraging within the commonwealth the establishment of a commonwealth loan plan for the assistance of countries within the commonwealth, because represented within the commonwealth are almost all the races and colours of men. What the minister has said, in effect, is that Canada, as a leading nation desiring peace and the raising of standards throughout the world, accepts her responsibility as nations must today as being their brother's keeper.
In so far as the general purport of what he has said is concerned, there will be widespread approval. The particulars, however, will require examination to the end that in any contribution we make internationally in this regard, first consideration should be given to the commonwealth countries.

maintopic: DEBATES-CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXPANSION OF ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is quite correct when he says
Expansion of Economic Assistance that the bulk of the Canadian people will support a generous program of aid to the underdeveloped and emerging nations of the world. I believe they will welcome the announcement which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made regarding proposed increases in Canada's assistance in the coming fiscal year.
However, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has such a marvellous capacity for wrapping up any gifts in tinsel, fancy ribbon and gift packaging that one might tend to be a little deceived as to just how much is in the package. Even after the increases which are proposed for the coming fiscal year, Canada's aid to underdeveloped countries will amount to less than one half of one per cent of our gross national product, and part of this amount of some $185 million to $190 million will be in the form of loans at low interest rates, so that it will not be entirely a gift.
I was surprised that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made mention of the assistance given to the Caribbean countries which have passed through very difficult times in recent months as a result of tornadoes. Our contribution to the entire Caribbean area was $20,000 in cash and skim milk powder worth about $80,000. This is a total contribution in cash and kind of about $100,000 to cover several countries which suffered very serious damage.
The government and the people of Canada have to take seriously this question of economic aid to underdeveloped areas. The latest figures available show that the share of the world's goods which goes to these nations is less now than it was before the war. It is greater in total, but in terms of the share of the world's total production it is less, because western production has grown so rapidly that the underdeveloped areas are today getting a smaller share of the world's total production than they used to get.
If the world is to have any hope of living at peace, then we must be prepared to spend more money assisting these underdeveloped areas. In the long run this will do more to maintain peace in the world than will the billions of dollars which the western world is spending on armaments. Many of these countries not only require immediate assistance but their most crying need is for capital and capital equipment, so they can increase their productivity and raise the living standards of their people.
We in this party welcome the announcement which has been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but we think that even with this small increase we are doing far less than we ought to be doing.

Expansion of Economic Assistance We should not be satisfied with anything less than 1 per cent of our gross national product, and we in this party have for years advocated that our goal should be 2 per cent of Canada's gross national product as an investment in peace and in bringing economic prosperity to the underdeveloped areas of the world. We contend that the best hope for future generations to live in peace lies in this kind of aid, and that we ought to be diverting more of our money in this direction.

maintopic: DEBATES-CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXPANSION OF ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made this announcement today. Certainly any increase in the aid we can give to those in a less favoured position than our own is to be commended, but I am concerned that even though this word is encouraging it is still only a very small part of what we could and should be doing.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has mentioned that this will be adding something more than 50 per cent to the budget for this particular type of aid in the coming fiscal year. Even at that, and considering the statistics he gave to us yesterday, it will bring us only to approximately one half of what is being given per capita by the United Kingdom and West Germany, and only to a quarter of what is being given by the citizens of the United States and France. This is not good enough. I think we should realize that it is not only our moral obligation but it is also our privilege to be in a position where we can be doing more, and it is not to our credit that more is not being done.
I note with interest the areas to which this assistance will be given, and I agree with previous speakers that it is our first obligation to the commonwealth countries to prove that the spirit of understanding and good will that we have in the commonwealth should express itself in the type of assistance afforded in the Colombo plan that we have known so well down through the years. It is of particular interest that this assistance will be aimed to further helping the Caribbean area. I think this is a timely opportunity for us, because this is an area right on our own doorstep which is part of a volatile situation that could blow up at any time as far as Latin America and the neighbouring area of central America are concerned. It is an area where we could be making a total contribution that would really do some good. I trust the government will see fit to still further increase the aid that they suggest be given to the Caribbean area.
It is good, also, that we have Africa in mind. The Secretary of State for External

Affairs spoke of Latin America, and certainly there is no more needy part of the world than this. I wonder whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs might be considering tying in this materialistic assistance with the moral aid for which the people of Latin America have been looking for a long time, in our becoming a member of the organization of American states. I think this is a very important question, and we cannot very much longer avoid taking a decision on it.
I suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that one of the greatest developed resources we have as Canadians is that reserve of good will which Canadian people have created for themselves and for their country. We should be making sure this resource is exploited to the maximum in considering this program of aid.
I also suggest that in planning the distribution of this aid we should make sure that it goes to areas where the assistance can make a distinct contribution in the field in which it is needed. It is not just in giving away that we can help these countries. Therefore I think it is a good thing that financial assistance is being made possible at no interest cost. We have this ability to help other people help themselves. I think this is a phase of aid which is not considered often enough. It is not just a hand-out that is wanted; it is assistance that will help people help themselves.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we support wholeheartedly what has been said here today, but we do hope it is only a small part of what is to come in the future.

maintopic: DEBATES-CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXPANSION OF ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people will, I am sure, welcome the announcement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) to the effect that Canada's assistance to underdeveloped countries will be $190 million, that is an increase of $1-40 million over the contribution of the past few years. Canadians are anxious to help the have-not countries in the world through their government.
Canada's economic aid to underdeveloped countries will take the form of financial and technical assistance. As stated by those who spoke before me, financial aid is important but technical assistance is even more important since it enables the recipient countries to initiate projects, for if those countries need our financial help, they need above all the means to become self-supporting eventually. That is how we can contribute to the protection of those countries against subversive ideas.

We have been contributing to the Colombo plan for years. I am quite in favour of helping certain members of the commonwealth, that is certain, hard-pressed Caribbean countries. When I was in Jamaica, over a year ago, I saw people who wanted not so much our credit to purchase products as our technical assistance to improve their condition. Those countries have their own natural resources and they can develop themselves if we show them how and if we help them.
Now, it is a fine thing to help those countries, but I should like to remind the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that we still have in Canada areas which are underdeveloped and where people experience hard times in the midst of abundance. We approve and we commend this assistance to the underdeveloped countries but the government should also have some thought for the Canadians who contribute to the development of this country of ours.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Secretary of State for External Affairs say what the decision has been regarding recognition of the provisional revolutionary government of South Viet Nam. What are the considerations that impelled the government to its decision, and would the minister deal in general with the ominous situation in that country consequent upon the change of administration?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SOUTH VIET NAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
Inquiries of the Ministry gentleman was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question. When he asked me the other day about this matter I was not in a position to deal with it, for a number of reasons. One was that there had been no request for recognition from the provisional government of the republic of Viet Nam.
Since then such a request has been received and this question has been examined. The government has decided to accord recognition to the government of the republic of Viet Nam. The considerations which the Canadian government examined were: The fact that the government is in actual control of the major part of the territory of the state; it has undertaken to observe international obligations entered into by its predecessors, and it has secured the acquiescence of the population. It has also promised to protect foreign lives and property and to guarantee fundamental freedoms "within the framework of the anti-communist struggle and the security of the state". Moreover, the Vietnamese government has undertaken to maintain co-operation with the international supervisory commission on which Canada serves.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subsubtopic: CANADIAN REACTION TO PROPOSED EMBARGO
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Can the minister advise the house why the Canadian United Nations delegation did not support the resolution so strongly endorsed yesterday by the assembly, calling for an embargo on oil shipments to South Africa?

maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subsubtopic: CANADIAN REACTION TO PROPOSED EMBARGO
speechtext:
The Canadian delegation fully supported the basic aims of the resolution to which the hon. member directs my attention. We support, in principle, its reaffirmation of the right of the people of South West Africa to self determination and independence, and its condemnation of South Africa's persistent refusal to co-operate with the United Nations. We were in favour of a renewed effort to establish the United Nations presence in South West Africa.
The Canadian delegate pointed out yesterday that the imposition of sanctions in specific cases is a matter which, under the charter, reposes in the security council and not in the general assembly. Moreover, in the view of the Canadian government enforcement action by the United Nations should await the outcome of the proceedings presently before the international court as well as the reaction of the South African government to the findings of that court. In our view it weakens rather than strengthens the United Nations if such important principles of orderly procedure are disregarded.

I should like to emphasize the deep concern felt by this government about developments in South Africa. We deplore the application by that government of the policy of apartheid in South West Africa, where it has a duty to administer the territory under international authority in the best interests of the population. The present serious situation could develop in such a way as to call for support by Canada of measures in accordance with the provisions of the United Nations charter to enforce respect for international obligations.

TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, October 2, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. MacEachen-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
That it is expedient, as a means toward the further development of manpower in Canada and toward increasing employment opportunities for Canadians, to introduce a measure to amend the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act:
[Mr. Macdonald 1
(a)	to provide that in respect of the costs incurred by a province as training allowances for unemployed persons, the contributions payable by Canada to the province be increased from 75 per cent to such percentage, not exceeding 90 per cent, as may be specified in the agreement made under the act between the Minister of Labour and the province:
(b)	to provide in respect of the costs incurred by the province for such part of the program for training employed persons in industry as may be specified in the agreement, the contributions payable by Canada to the province be increased from 50 to 75 per cent thereof;
(c)	to extend, until such date as may be specified in the agreement made under the act between the Minister of Labour and the province, the period during which the contributions payable by Canada to the province will be 75 per cent in respect of costs incurred by the province for capital expenditures on training facilities; and
(d)	to increase the number of members of the technical and vocational training advisory council from twenty three to twenty eight and to provide an honorarium for the chairman thereof.

maintopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the government introduced this resolution for consideration by this house on October 2, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Kootenay East, made a statement on behalf of the minister. Amongst other things that day he said this resolution set forth the government's new employment and manpower development program. This is indeed a surprise, when the government describes this resolution as a new employment and manpower development program. This has been the habit of the government since it took office, to adopt all those good programs that were put on the statute books of this country and camouflage them to the extent that they describe them as new. Later on he said these measures are designed to improve the federal-provincial program of technical and vocational education.
Well, there is nothing in the statement or in the resolution itself to show what the improvement will be, except that the government is agreeing by this alteration of the existing legislation to increase the federal contribution. I should like to deal with this matter item by item as set out in the resolution.
I want to say, first of all, that this resolution does not introduce any new or improved legislation. All it does is raise the federal government's contribution in order to carry on the program the Conservative government initiated and pressed forward from 1960 on. I immediately say to you, Mr. Chairman, that this last observation of mine is generally looked upon in this session of parliament as a sort of partisan statement. There seems to be a new point of view in parliament, at least this session, that partisanship should not have any place in this house. Well, I recall

the days when government members were sitting on this side of the house, and they claimed that if partisanship had no place in parliament then parliament would almost die on its feet. I think it is only normal and natural that those who are in the opposition should criticize the government, and should also take advantage of the opportunity to point out that they inaugurated programs of this type when they had the opportunity.
1 feel, too, that when one is referring to what has been done in the past the record should be kept straight, and that any misleading or camouflaging statements by this government should be challenged. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour went on in his statement to say that the provision of capital facilities for the training of youths and adults under the Technical and Vocational Training Act of 1960 is far from complete in many of the provinces. It is therefore important to continue a high level of federal financial assistance to those provinces which still need to develop extensive training facilities.
In this statement there is an admission by the government that this is not a new program, but rather that the program should be continued in order to provide additional facilities in those provinces that did not avail themselves of that opportunity in the period from April, 1961 to March 31, 1963. However, it is regrettable that in his statement the parliamentary secretary failed to set out what has been done in this school building program since that time.
Before we launched into this program we asked the provinces to set out what they considered would be their facility needs for the next five years, and it is interesting to note their responses to this query. Newfoundland stated that it would need some $6,300,000 worth of facilities, Prince Edward Island $750,000, Nova Scotia $9 million, New Brunswick $9.5 million, Quebec $53.5 million, Ontario $50 million, Manitoba $9.5 million, Saskatchewan $6.5 million, Alberta $28 million and British Columbia $19 million.
We of course set out to plan and provide for these needs. What has happened since then? There has been a total projects estimated cost of $511,274,390, and the federal government contribution has amounted to over $326 million. A total of 519 projects were completed in that time, including 254 new schools, four technical institutions and 47 trade schools, providing space for some 138,000 students each and every year.
When this program was nearing completion the ministers of education for the provinces met with me here in Ottawa, and only the province of Quebec felt it had not had its full share of the program. It was pointed out
Vocational Training Assistance Act to Quebec that there was no ceiling set on the amount of money available for the construction program, but that it was left to each province to proceed with its required needs as it foresaw them during that period of time. I may immediately say all but one of the provinces signed the agreement with the federal government some time in April, 1961, but Quebec did not sign an agreement until six months later. Therefore it is understandable that Quebec did not proceed as rapidly with this program as some of the other provinces, particularly Ontario.
In his statement the parliamentary secretary set out the policy to guide the federal government in its contribution of 75 per cent, and the basis upon which this contribution would be considered, having as a ceiling $480 per capita applicable to the population in the age bracket of 15 to 19 years. Evidently this has been based on the amount of construction which has been carried out in the province of Newfoundland.
I decided to work out how much money would be available to each province as a result of this new formula, having in mind what the federal government had already contributed to this program ending on March 31, 1963. It is discovered that from now until March 31, 1967, Newfoundland will have been overpaid by some $17,000. Prince Edward Island will have some $2 million in contributions from the federal government coming to it in the next four years. Nova Scotia will have $24 million coming to it, and New Brunswick will have a credit of some $20.5 million. Quebec will have a credit of $199 million, Ontario $9 million, Manitoba $29 million, Saskatchewan $26.5 million, Alberta $10.5 million and British Columbia $40.5 million. The Northwest Territories will receive some $751,000 and the Yukon will have been overpaid or overdrawn on this program by some $312,000.
These figures are approximate, but when you examine them you will note that some of the smaller provinces in the maritimes will have a sizeable credit coming to them between now and 1967. But you must also consider that they have to put up 25 per cent of the cost of construction of these schools. Therefore the question arises to what extent will these provinces avail themselves of this program in addition to what they have already done? How far can they extend their financial resources to take advantage of this program?
Ontario certainly cannot do very much. All that is left coming to it is some $9 million, so its building program between now and

Vocational Training Assistance Act 1967 will be very slight. Quebec is the outstanding province and can avail itself of some $199 million in federal contributions. It is all well and good.
In the field of training the unemployed, and this has been a very worth while effort, we increased the federal contribution by 25 per cent. Until 1960 very little training was carried out in this area. In the year 1959-60 some 4,638 people were trained; in 1960-61 this figure increased to 10,774 because of the increased federal contribution to the provinces; in 1961-62 the number of applicants trained was 26,887. Then in the last year, 1962-63, some 38,439 people were trained. One might reasonably criticize this figure and say it is not sufficient, and I would be inclined to agree. I think this program is very worth while and should be accentuated. However, one can immediately see that the action taken in 1960 has increased the number of people trained under this program by some 34,000. This is indeed a worth while program; because those who find themselves unemployed, whether they are young or more elderly, can benefit from the courses that are provided under this program.
Under this resolution the government proposes to increase its share by 15 per cent; that is to say, from 75 per cent to 90 per cent. I would like to spend just a moment or two making some observations in respect to this program of training the unemployed. It has always been a puzzle to me why this program was not endorsed by organized labour, and particularly the Canadian Labour Congress. In reverse, however, there has been a great deal of criticism stemming from some hon. members. It was pointed out at one time that this program was so unco-ordinated that in one instance nine welders were trained by an experienced welder and then they all became unemployed. This story was repeated in the election campaign by some hon. members who now sit on the treasury benches. I think they did a great disservice to this program, because I think if everyone co-ordinated their efforts to make it successful, many thousands of Canadians would benefit.
I would like to cite as an example the city of Cornwall. This city was left in the position where it had a great many unemployed after the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway, first of all, and then because of the closing down of a textile mill. However, people were not despondent about the situation. They gathered together and organized, and every part of their economy grouped together in one combined effort. They were able-and they did not have to try very hard-to persuade the provincial and federal governments

to take part of this mill, convert it into classrooms and provide $85,000 worth of equipment in order to retrain their people. I think 800 people were retrained, and 90 per cent of them were placed in jobs as a result of that retraining program in this area. The amazing thing is that the program that was instituted in Cornwall brought to that city two new industries, because they were able to train people and provide the skills required by those industries. Therefore I think all of us in this country should give encouragement to this program in order to help those who need new skills and trades.
I attended the opening of this training school in Cornwall, and I was very much impressed to find a gentleman who was 62 years of age working on a lathe alongside a young man 19 years of age. I was curious about the elderly gentleman and asked him whether he was learning machine work at his age. He said "I used to be a machinist in the old days, but I have not engaged in this trade for quite a number of years. However, I find myself unemployed and I am here taking this course in order to brush up, because I now have a job available to me". So this program is not just for the purpose of training young people; it has had the effect of inducing older citizens to take part in this retraining program in order to reinstate themselves in employment.
There are a number of things in this resolution to which we could refer. One is paragraph (b), under which the government proposes to increase by 25 per cent its contribution to the provinces for the training of employed persons. This is very necessary. We started a pilot project in the town of Leaside, in which three industries each contributed ten employees, making a total of 30 students, in order that they might upgrade themselves and learn those skills that were required for this upgrading. I think that pilot project will be of great help to industry in the retraining of people in order to provide them with better jobs and consequently better financial remuneration.
I think this program is one that will be the basis in our battle, in the war that we are waging to provide jobs for Canadians and to alleviate the unemployment situation in this country. I think we have taken forward steps in this regard. I do hope that the provinces will avail themselves of this additional 15 per cent increase, to 90 per cent, and establish more training centres in order to provide training facilities for those who find themselves unemployed. Education is a very worth while thing. Not very many years ago we in this country particularly were stressing the three "R's" type of education; that is to

say, in the academic field. It has been somewhat difficult to sell people this new type of education upon which we launched in 1960. However, I think people now understand that every person in this country cannot apply himself to academic training, but many have certain skills with their hands and could usefully perform these skills. We must of necessity provide this opportunity.
For many thousands of Canadians education is the frontier of the future, and I feel certain that technical and vocational training forms a very essential part of that frontier. I had always believed that in no single field is a concerted, co-operative effort on the part of provinces and the federal government of more importance to the future of the development of our country in this regard. Education, of course, is subject to fads, just as any other branch of human endeavour, and for many years a classical and academic education represented the ultimate achievement for many young people in this country. But the pendulum has swung back in the last few years, and there is a new emphasis on those branches of knowledge relating to the technical and the practical which in the past were neglected except for the efforts of a few pioneers. One need only travel across the country today and visit some of these schools which have been opening and are opening at this moment to receive a tremendous revelation at what is being done. One would be very impressed indeed at the enthusiasm of those who are taking their places in these schools and learning the skills and trades afforded to them.
Criticism was made at the beginning to the effect that many of these schools would be half empty, that the enrolment would be insufficient to fill the classrooms. On the contrary, most of the schools which have been opened have waiting lists, and I think this condition will be accentuated. Certainly where it is greatly accentuated the provincial authorities should take steps to provide more facilities for those who want to avail themselves of this type of education.
There is a new recognition, Mr. Chairman, of the place in society of those whose genius is along practical lines. Opportunity is being provided for those who are doers as well as those who are thinkers. This is only fitting in face of the impressive and revolutionary accomplishments of the physical and technological sciences in recent years. In the physical sciences man, having spanned the earth, has now taken the first step toward spanning the universe. In technology we are moving toward a state of affairs where new electronic and mechanical processes will eliminate the routine processes of production in so far as men and women are concerned.
Vocational Training Assistance Act But in that elimination of what is routine will be posed the challenge to our working force to adapt itself to operations demanding skills of a high technical quality. This, of course, means the acquirement of basic skills and a high degree of adaptability and mobility in our labour force.
I said earlier in my remarks, Mr. Chairman, that we are providing an educational plant capacity for more than 139,000 additional students. This is over the accommodation which was available only three years ago. A program of this type cannot be conceived in terms of money alone. This has cost the federal treasury many hundreds of millions of dollars, but it is a worth while expenditure when we are investing in the future of our citizens. When we do that we are investing in the future of our country. Therefore I say that this program must not be conceived only in terms of money but in terms of what it can accomplish in the upgrading of our labour force and in bringing about a condition where those in the labour force, rather than being at the mercy of the sudden shifts and changes of the automation age, will be able to play a constantly expanding role in production.
I must repeat that during the last parliament we introduced a bill, No. C-83, with respect to industrial change and manpower adjustment. In doing that I thought we were moving in the right direction to deal with those who would be displaced by automation. We tried to make that bill as flexible as possible in order to fit into the conditions of any industry which would avail itself of the services thus provided. We felt that we must bring to the attention of those who would be affected by such technological change the services available to them under the bill, and we intended to do this by calling a national conference of employers and unions in order that they would have the opportunity, based on their own experience, to offer to us suggestions upon which we would base our regulations in respect thereto. I only regret that the government has seen fit to abandon this item of legislation.

I can only regret, Mr. Chairman, that the government has not seen fit to reintroduce that bill but rather is proceeding now under agreements with the provinces. I do not think it will have the same success in capturing the imagination of the people of this

Vocational Training Assistance Act country as had the previous bill, which received many favourable comments from all parts of the country and from all segments of our economy.
These programs for conducting training cannot be treated each one in isolation. They must all be taken together and dovetailed in mutually complementary fashion. However, I am sure that with the progress we are making in providing training facilities across the country, in placing trained students in the working force, in encouraging industry to produce in Canada, and in encouraging labour and management to work together to cope with the far reaching shifts and changes which must be faced if we are to remain competitive-with all these things we are working toward a better and brighter world of tomoi'row in which those who are engaged in production will offer a contribution which will be both more efficient and more valuable to the economy as a whole.
I should like to say at this time, Mr. Chairman, that I feel that boards of education in our cities, towns and areas of our townships who play a part in the construction of these particular vocational schools, in addition to the high schools, should be congratulated for their co-operation and their clear-sightedness in launching upon this program in co-operation with the federal and provincial governments.
The teaching staffs have been a problem in this whole area. For those provinces which availed themselves of the opportunity offered by the federal government in its contribution of 50 per cent toward the cost of training those teachers there has not been as much difficulty as others have experienced. It was reasonable to assume that there would be a shortage of teachers, because when you are providing only the short space of time which has been provided under this program you must certainly launch yourselves on a crash training program of teachers. But that is not the only profession in which we have a shortage in this country. There is a continuing shortage of nurses, and there are shortages in other fields of endeavour as well. I think we have done well in providing teachers to staff these schools.
These are in total my remarks today. I hope the government does not lose its drive. I hope it does not allow the momentum in this area to diminish, but that the Department of Labour and its minister will keep on top of all these things and encourage the provinces to take advantage of these incentives which the federal government has offered during all these years.

maintopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hope has been expressed that at the resolution stage of this bill a contribution by one speaker from each party

will suffice. We agree, on the understanding that there will be no such voluntary restriction of debate on second reading. I am sure a number of hon. members will speak at that time.
It is the responsibility of this parliament to strengthen the capacities of our people in order that they may make a maximum contribution to our economic growth and our cultural advancement. I and my colleagues in the New Democratic party are pleased to support this resolution, which is designed to improve existing provisions for vocational and technical training across this nation. Education, not of the few but of the masses, is essential in the twentieth century. To attain this objective there is urgent need of more facilities and more effective training of our young people. Today, Canadians are not a well educated people. According to recent labour statistics only 32 per cent of our students complete high school; fewer than 10 per cent enter university; only 4 per cent graduate from an institution of higher learning.
In the technical field the story is the same. Canada has never trained enough manpower to meet the needs of industry. One out of every three Canadian youngsters leaves school totally unprepared for work. This constitutes a national catastrophe. The real tragedy lies not so much in the cost of unemployment and welfare benefits but in the loss to the nation of the abilities of mind and hand of thousands of able young people. In five skilled occupations recently studied, one third of the men were trained outside this country. Records indicate, too, that the flow of this type of immigrant is slowing up because of favourable economic conditions in Europe.
The following editorial appeared in the Globe and Mail of July 6, 1963:
Education has so consistently held the spotlight of attention during the past few years that most people have been under the impression that Canada was taking large strides in the field, and that the children of the nation were being graduated into the working force with more and better education than ever before. It comes as a shock, therefore, to discover that the number of school dropouts is on the increase and that more young people are being turned out every year without the education or the skills to make an adequate living.
This gloomy picture emerges from a survey conducted by the Ontario department of education and the national employment service of students who leave school early, and of their employment prospects. The survey discloses that 36.4 per cent of students, who left school in Ontario in 1962, earned neither certificate nor diploma.
The employment side of the survey indicates that the fate of these early school-leavers is to spend their lives chasing unskilled and semi-skilled jobs in a world where such jobs are becoming progressively fewer and in which they can look forward, therefore, to frequent periods of unemployment.

What can we do to raise educational standards among the working force of Canada? In seeking an answer I suggest seven points as worthy of consideration by educational authorities:
1.	Parents must express an appreciation of the value of education in terms of employment and future happiness and income. Youth must be convinced that to be uneducated is to be handicapped for life. They should be told that only 30 per cent of the jobs in Canada are available to the unskilled or semi-skilled workers, and the number is decreasing rapidly with the advancement of automation. Recently Professor Marcus Long of Toronto predicted that automation will make any student without grade XII education unemployable within ten years. Young people should be encouraged to remain in school until they possess skills that are currently in demand.
2.	Greater prestige must be associated with occupational education in Canada. Unfortunately, too many people are inclined to look down on hand work even in a very specialized field. We should remember that our complex society cannot function without many different varieties of highly trained personnel. Without downgrading academic achievement we should elevate the status of the skilled artisan. Prejudices by parents against vocational courses are foolish and antiquated. They try to make professional types out of boys best fitted to become mechanics, technicians and tradesmen. Too frequently, as a result, they end up academic failures and embittered unemployed.
3.	A critical assessment needs to be made of the courses of study in our vocational and technical schools. Narrow specialization to the exclusion of general knowledge should be avoided in order that the student may develop a flexibility of mind that permits a shift from one job to another with a minimum of difficulty. His training needs to be as up to date as possible and related to the dominant needs and interests of the community in which he lives.
4.	More qualified teachers and administrators should be attracted to the new technical schools which are being opened across Canada. It is urgent that we should train an increasing number of science teachers if we are to take advantage of the fast developing technological revolution in North America.
5.	Importance of continuing education must be emphasized for all ages. More facilities for trade and occupational classes at post-high school level should be provided. In an era of rapid change there is no better insurance for the worker and the citizen than to improve
Vocational Training Assistance Act his skills and add to his knowledge and experience at every opportunity.
6.	Training programs will be successful only if there is the closest co-operation between federal and provincial authorities in the field of education. The final decision in such matters must always rest with the provinces. There must be no suspicion of domination by Ottawa.
7.	Closer partnership is needed between the school and industry. The activities of the classroom should be co-ordinated with those of the workshop. According to a recent report only 31 per cent of manufacturing establishments in Canada had any training program at all designed to assist a boy to fit into his first job.
In a recent article entitled "Employers' Role in Job Training", J. Bascom St. John wrote as follows:
Far too little responsibility for the transition from school to work is taken by employers. An incredibly small proportion of them have any special training program, or any system of induction into work methods or skills.
They take a boy from school, let him flounder in an unfamiliar environment and if he does not happen to light on his feet they get rid of him. Nothing the school might have done, or could do, will get over the problem of the irresponsible employer. No guidance program or teaching pattern can prevent the harm that selfish employers do when the schoolboy enters the world of work.
We expect far too much from our schools if we assume they can do the whole job of work training. You learn the techniques of work by working, and it is through a partnership between the schools and employment that the most effective progress may be made in meeting the needs of skill and the special training for work in the technological era.
The question of the relationship between education, work, citizenship and national economic and employment policies cuts through all aspects of our society. The schools ought not to be asked to carry the burdens that other interests are too lazy or too unimaginative to deal with.
Finally, I wish to say that facilities relating to training in the occupational field are as important to the future economic strength and social well-being of Canadians as those in the areas of secondary and higher education. All obstacles must be removed to permit not only youth but men and women of any age to take full advantage of the educational opportunities available in this country. If we are wise we shall determine to provide for these purposes in the future a larger percentage of our gross national product than we have been willing to do in the past. Education must be given a higher priority in our national thinking and our national planning.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel the members from Quebec must give very special attention to the resolution under consideration

Vocational Training Assistance Act which would amend the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act.
I cannot but take advantage of this opportunity to point out the complaints of the province of Quebec in connection with that act. It is unfair and discriminatory with regard to Quebec, and if the minister does not make the necessary changes, we shall bring in amendments to protect the interests of the province of Quebec.
The Quebec minister of youth, the Hon. Paul Gerin-Lajoie, released last winter a statement regarding the capital expenditures contemplated under that act, from April 1 to November 5, 1962. The figures quoted by the minister are revealing; they show that Quebec's share is only 3.3 per cent of the total number of students covered by that act throughout Canada, whereas Ontario's share amounts to 73.1 per cent.
Out of a total of $511 million-and these are recent figures published by Ottawa-the province of Quebec got only $25 million, or 5 per cent of the total, whereas Ontario got over $200 million, or 40 per cent of the total.
We claim it is unfair that our province should have to pay its share of federal taxes, when other provinces benefit from them to a larger extent.
Mr. Chairman, that act, which was passed in 1960 and gives such results, works entirely against the interests of the province of Quebec because it is based on discriminatory and unfair principles. In fact, as it stands now, that act is tailored according to the needs of the English system in the other provinces of Canada and does not suit the province of Quebec whose education system is entirely different.
In Ontario, for instance-and I suppose also in other English speaking provinces-secondary vocational schools are part of the high school system. In that case, the federal law applies, and we see that the province of Ontario received grants enabling it to build almost 200 high schools and vocational schools.
In Quebec, secondary educational institutions, like elementary schools, are not under the government but under the public education council. In that province, vocational schools, whether they be trade schools or other schools, are not considered government institutions as in other provinces. Consequently, if federal grants cannot be used for technological institutes and trades schools, in the province of Quebec, whereas they are used also for secondary vocational schools in Ontario and other English speaking provinces, we have here a discrimination which the Liberal and Conservative members let go through at the time.
It is therefore not suprising that the province of Quebec is unable to take full

advantage of the federal technical and vocational training program, because its educational and professional training system differs from that of other provinces.
Here is what the Quebec minister of youth, the Hon. Paul Gerin-Lajoie, had to say on that point at a meeting in Dorion, last March:
The problem with regard to federal assistance in the building of training centres is the following:
1.	Ottawa contributes in the same degree to the financing of training centres and to the financing of technical and vocational schools;
2.	The federal contribution is always proportional to the provincial government contribution;
3.	In every province except Quebec, training centres are subsidized by the provincial government only;
4.	In Quebec, however, the apprenticeship centres are developed not only with Quebec subsidies, but also with subsidies from the apprenticeship commission, a joint employer-employee body unparalleled in Canada;
5.	Therefore, Ottawa subsidizes apprenticeship centres in Quebec only according to the provincial government contributions and not according to the total grants paid out to training centres.
In the light of the treatment meted out to Quebec, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie speaks of discrimination.
"To date, the federal government has refused to contribute to the financing of apprenticeship centres in Quebec to the same extent as it does to the financing of technical and vocational schools.
Ottawa does not take into account the expenditures made by the Quebec apprenticeship commission out of its revenues for the setting up of apprenticeship centres."
The minister responsible for education said that an end must be put to such discrimination at any cost; indeed it is a repetition of the one created by Ottawa's refusal to continue for a certain period its 75 per cent contribution to technical and vocational training in general. Because of that refusal, the contribution is brought back to 50 per cent: without Quebec having had by far the same opportunity as Ontario to take advantage of supplementary grants.
Then, stressing the importance of the report of the committee for the study of technical and vocational training, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie came to the conclusion that the main thing was to adapt our educational system to the needs of our economic development.
In conjunction with economic development, we must, he said, "train our young people in relation to the special requirements of modern industry and business.. .So, I find it particularly significant that the first building under construction in the first youth centre should be a training establishment, precisely an institution where education and work are directly related."
Here is, Mr. Chairman, another statement published in Le Devoir of February 16, 1963, which reads as follows:
Deficiencies in federal assistance to vocational training. Grits and Tories in Ottawa largely responsible.
In Ontario and other provinces, some form of vocational training is given in vocational schools which are part and parcel of the high school system. In Quebec, vocational training and technical courses are given in trade schools, training centres and technological institutes which are not part of the high school system.
Consequently, Ontario has been able to use-
At that time, that is on February 16, 1963.

-$186,700,000 from the federal treasury to build and improve 207 vocational schools, 7 technological institutes and 14 trades schools to meet the needs of a school population of 93,056 students.
On the other hand, the province of Quebec was able to use only $13,600,000 in federal funds to build 3 institutes...
...To give justice to all the provinces, the federal government has only to amend its act and I would say that it should.
It can do so in various ways. First, it can adopt an equalization formula or use the formula which existed previously in that field: giving federal grants in relation to the number of students or young workers between 14 and 19 in each province.
Another way to right an obvious injustice with regard to Quebec is to allow it to receive federal grants for training centers now in existence.
Here is what the Quebec minister of youth stated in Quebec city at the conference of the education ministers of the ten provinces:
The minister of youth said yesterday that the decision of the federal Minister of Labour to extend for six months only the agreement by which Ottawa pays 75 per cent of the construction cost of technical and vocational training schools is a provocation.
That federal contribution was to be reduced to 50 per cent by April 1, 1963; but the education ministers from all the provinces had asked for a continuation of the 75 per cent contribution until 1967.
To that request, the federal minister, Mr. Michael Starr answered on Thursday by offering a six month extension for works started before October 1 and for which contracts had been awarded before April 1.
Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie, chairman of the conference of the education ministers of the ten provinces stated yesterday that Mr. Starr's decision did not meet in any way the request made by all the provinces.
"As far as Quebec is concerned," he added, "far from being a solution to the problem, such a decision appears as a provocation. It will favour even more the provinces which are already engaged in a large construction program."
In fact, explained the minister, as far as the development of technical training is concerned, Quebec finds itself today in the situation which confronted the province of Ontario in April 1961.
"Moreover," said Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, "it must be realized that the implementation of a vast program of physical development in the field of technical education (which will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and will mortgage the future for many years) must not be considered as an obstacle race between the provinces".
Federal moneys should not be intended as a reward to provinces succeeding in completing as soon as possible a building program-especially not when they are in an uneven position at the start.
The federal program for assistance to technical training should be designed rather as a means to solve the problem of labour training throughout the country.
In order to achieve this goal, the ministers of education of the ten provinces jointly urged the federal government to review the existing agreement.
Mr. Chairman, there is another point of divergence between the province of Quebec and the other provinces; this difference can be found also in the concept of vocational training.
Vocational Training Assistance Act
Vocational and technical training means any kind of education aimed at preparing a person for a profitable job in a primary or secondary industry or a profitable employment in the service industry, or at increasing his skill or technical ability in a similar job or employment. And, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, this includes the training thus directed in relation to any of the following industries or employments: agriculture, fishing, forestry, manufacturing, mining, communications and, as a general rule, any primary or secondary industry or any employment in a service industry which asks for a knowledge of scientific and technical principles, and their application.
Therefore, any intelligent person can conclude that vocational training, whether it is given in factories, in private institutions or in state schools, qualifies as vocational training within the meaning of the present legislation.
There is in the province of Quebec a vocational training system which is controlled not by the department of youth but by the department of labour.
Under the jurisdiction of the department of labour, there are training centres for all building trades in Montreal, Sherbrooke, Quebec city, Joliette and Chicoutimi. There is a school for shoe workers in Montreal and other vocational training institutions of a public character, for they do not belong to individuals but to professional bodies.
Those professional institutions give a better vocational training, according to several experts, than the state-owned trade schools and institutes of technology.
In 1960, 846 regular day students attended the only building trades school in Montreal, and since this centre was built in 1946, 15,446 apprentices and journeymen have taken refresher courses.
It should be recalled that since that date, this body has contributed $4,044,314 to provide vocational training for construction workers, while the contribution of the provincial government was only $375,000, or an annual subsidy of $25,000.
Now, there are no real vocational schools in the other provinces. As a result, there is no provision in the present federal legislation for a federal contribution or assistance to those schools. This is discriminatory to the province of Quebec which has very special institutions that it intends to preserve and with which employers and workers are entirely satisfied.
Mr. Chairman, since the resolution does not contain anything to make up this deficiency in the act, I move, seconded by Mr. Gauthier:
That this house urge the federal government to hand back to the provinces, except those which prefer the status quo, a percentage of the income
4736	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Assistance Act tax equal to the amounts the federal government would otherwise pay them as its contribution to the vocational and technical training assistance program, in order to enable the provinces to set up their own vocational training system as they see fit.
The amendment is in French and in English. The English version is a translation of the original amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a few brief remarks only on Bill S-28, to incorporate the Allstate Life Insurance Company of Canada.
This company seems to take advantage of the legislation recently adopted providing that when the degree of ownership of companies is 25 per cent Canadian, these companies may be considered as Canadian.
Actually, we do not wish to prevent transactions in the insurance field or in any other field, but to state our views about this inflow of American capital, because in fact, the Allstate company is 87J per cent controlled by Americans and only 12J per cent Canadian owned.

Private Bills
We have been told that the assets of the company are made up of 25 per cent of Canadian capital and 75 per cent of American capital. However, if it is considered that the company which holds 25 per cent of the Canadian capital is the Simpsons-Sears Company which is itself jointly owned by Canadians and by Americans on a 50-50 basis, that is its capital is made up of 50 per cent Canadian funds and 50 per cent American funds. This means that, actually, the Allstate Company of Canada is 87\ per cent controlled by Americans and only 12J per cent by Canadians.
We urge the Allstate company to increase Canadian representation on its board of directors and also the Canadian participation to 50 per cent of its assets or 50 per cent of its subscribed capital, so that we may have at least a 50 per cent Canadian company, because throughout the country, we are asked to encourage by all possible means the establishment of new Canadian companies. We are not asked to authorize the investment of new foreign capital in Canada but rather of Canadian capital which could be used for the expansion of our economy.
Insurance companies, and Allstate is no exception, are the second largest trust in Canada after the chartered banks. Therefore, we must take positive steps to prevent the American trust from taking over our economy through insurance companies or otherwise. That does not mean that we should close the door to foreign investments.
Still, we must force those people to make concessions which will raise economic standards in Canada because, in the final analysis, the important thing is the economic strength of Canada.
In this case, it is obvious that Allstate will pay taxes but it will still be making profits from the people and industry of Canada and this American company will make further profits from their investment in Canada.
As I said, we do not want to forbid completely foreign companies from settling in Canada. But we suggest to that particular company, as I mentioned before, that it increases the Canadian ownership in its assets.
In clause 1 of Bill S-28, we find the names of the citizens who make up that company: Messrs. John Atkinson, insurance executive; Edgar Gordon Burton, merchant; James Wilson Button, merchant; Gordon McCalla Graham, merchant; John James Illingworth, insurance executive and Norman Currie Urquhart, financier, all of the city of Toronto.
This company will have a part to play- actually it does play it now, and we all wonder why this bill is before us when this company already operates in Canada, holds a

federal licence to sell insurance in all Canadian provinces. In fact, we have seen for a long time Allstate advertised in the Simpsons-Sears catalogue. But we have before us today a bill to incorporate that insurance company which already holds a licence, and that without the matter having been submitted to the House of Commons. That company has therefore been operating until now. So, what advantages-there will certainly be no disadvantages-does that company anticipate in having this bill brought before us, if it operates in all the provinces?
We suggest to the company-and this is not separatism-to take into account the existence of two cultures in Canada, and to have among its directors both French and English Canadians, since it will operate, as it is already doing, in the province of Quebec as in the rest of Canada.
Those are suggestions we make to further improve the relations between the various ethnical groups but especially between the two major ethnical groups in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, this bill has no other purpose than to give recognition to a company which is 100 per cent American-owned and which is already in operation.
There is a slight improvement in that 12.5 per cent of the shares will be held by Canadians and 87.5 per cent by Americans.
I will say no more about the bill except that we strongly suggest that this proportion of 12.5 per cent should be increased gradually but as fast as possible until 50 per cent of the ownership and management of Allstate of Canada is in Canadian hands.

Mr. Chairman, I shall only take a few minutes.
On several occasions Bill S-28 concerning the Allstate Company has found its way on the order paper for consideration during the hour reserved for private members' business from five to six o'clock. We have repeatedly blocked the bill and we have stated our reasons for doing so.
We have now decided to allow the bill to pass if that is the wish of the house, and here is the reason why.
When we spoke against other legislation like, for instance, federal subsidies to the C.N.R., we had received representations from trucking associations or individual truck drivers who were backing us in our efforts.
When we objected to Bill S-7, an Act to incorporate the Pharmacy Examining Board of Canada, we were receiving lots of letters, telephone calls and messages encouraging us in our fight.
As concerns the Allstate Life Insurance Company bill, we never received a single remark, a single telephone call, a single letter,

a single message, from any insurance companies, insurance brokers or insurance agents whatever in Canada. This shows, in my opinion, that insurance companies that are Canadian to the extent of 100 per cent or 90 per cent, as well as insurance brokers or insurance agents, are not at all interested in the work we do in trying to prevent other insurance companies from getting a foothold in Canada, inasmuch as Canadian companies can very well look after all our insurance needs.
For these reasons, and also because we want to see what the work of the members of the other parties in this house will be in that respect, we have decided not to oppose any longer the adoption of this bill.
Mr. Chairman, we are still convinced that Canadians are able to look after the insurance needs of our country, but in view of the lack of co-operation on the part of insurance companies, brokers or agents, and their lack of interest in that matter, we have decided to let this bill pass.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill S-40, to incorporate Triassic Products Transmission Company.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to allow Pacific Petroleums to incorporate Triassic Products Transmission in order to return to Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, Vancouver, a similar federal charter which Westcoast had given to Pacific so it could construct without undue delay an important new Canadian industrial project. This $33.5 million project, now nearly completed, includes the building of the world's largest natural gas treatment plant at Empress, Alberta, and a 577 mile, 6 inch diameter pipe line from there to Winnipeg. The plant will process raw natural gas for the Trans-Canada Pipe Line Company by removing by-products, including propane, butane and ether liquid hydrocarbons. This is a necessary procedure and it results in the production of pure pipe line gas, methane, which is then moved by Trans-Canada to markets across the prairies and eastern Canada, and liquids, which will be moved through the new 577 mile unit.
Definitive plans to proceed with the project followed an agreement in 1961 between Pacific Petroleums and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. Engineering and preliminary work proceeded at once and plans were made to appear before the national energy board for a permit to proceed. However, the company had to be incorporated to appear before the board and to incorporate an interprovincial pipe line required a federal charter. Due to pressure of business in the House of Commons during the session that began in September, the company decided that it would be difficult to obtain a charter in time to commence construction. Pacific, therefore, requested of Westcoast Transmission that it receive no payment other than expenses for the loan of the federal charter of Petroleum Transmission Company which had been incorporated by Westcoast in 1955. Westcoast agreed to the transfer of the charter on the understanding that as soon as Pacific was able, it would request incorporation of a similar company and return-the borrowed charter-back to Westcoast. Thereupon the company appeared before the energy board and subsequently received permission to build.
Westcoast considers the return of a charter to be important to its business, particularly today when oil and gas exploration is expanding northward. Within a short time it is evpected that a movement of oil or liquid hydrocarbons may be contemplated from the Yukon or Northwest Territories.
Without a liquids pipe line, oil and by-products may be wasted in the production of natural gas. If Westcoast did not have this charter it could possibly face delays similar to those which would have been experienced by Pacific.
Westcoast Transmission Company, Vancouver, was incorporated by a federal act in 1949. This company, Canada's first major international pipe line, which went into operation in 1957, moved natural gas from northern Alberta and northern British Columbia down through British Columbia to the lower mainland and the Pacific northwest states. Building and operation of this pipe line has resulted in the greatest development northern Canada has ever seen. It is also an important factor in the development of the west and an important source of United States funds for Canada.
Pacific Petroleums was incorporated in British Columbia in 1942. This company is today one of Canada's major independent oil companies. Pacific found and pioneered the natural gas fields of British Columbia and for many years staked its future on the development of the north. Pacific sponsored Westcoast Transmission to bring these large new reserves to market, and it saw Westcoast through nine years of hearings in Alberta, Ottawa and Washington, D.C. Today the two companies have been entirely split apart with different management and different fields of operation. Pacific still maintains a share interest in Westcoast.
Both Pacific Petroleums and Westcoast Transmission qualify as companies 25 per cent of whose shares are available for purchase by Canadians.
Both companies were founded by Canadians, and shares have been traded since they began in business on Canadian stock exchanges. In the case of Westcoast it is 63.12 per cent Canadian owned. Pacific Petroleums is today 46 per cent owned by Phillips Petroleum Company, the remainder of these shares are available to Canadian purchasers. As of the moment, more than three million shares, representing 10,650 shareholders, are held in Canada.
