As hon. members are aware, the provisions with regard to the jurisdiction of the national energy board, and the procedure in that connection, make it essential that a special act of incorporation be passed by parliament so that the company may exercise the rights which the national energy board may grant to any particular company. Without purporting to have any expertise on this question, I simply suggest that perhaps this was the reason for the particular conduct engaged

in to which reference has been made. This indeed will be one of the questions which will be before the committee and upon which I am sure all hon. members will be interested in having some comment.
I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the general principles underlying the incorporation of companies of this kind, and their implications for the economy of Canada, and particularly for the economy of western Canada. Over the years hon. members have, I believe, noted with interest and with approval, the secondary implications of the growth of the oil industry in western Canada. I refer in particular to the utilization of those by-products which are produced in the process particularly of treating sour gas and the process of refining oil, which have resulted in the development of chemical components which it has been found possible to make available in a commercial way through industrial processes. With particular reference to the gas industry, I would refer in this connection to the development of a very substantial Canadian production of sulphur.
I believe I am right in saying that sulphur is one product which, no longer than a decade ago, was an essential Canadian import, a product which was in short supply in this country and which we had to import from abroad. As a result of the development of the Canadian oil industry, and particularly the development of secondary industry based on the oil industry, Canada has not only ceased to be a net importer of sulphur but has become a major exporter of this product. Under these circumstances, this particular product has been added to the list of products Canada sells abroad.
This, in turn, has had a particular importance for western Canada. Over the years, as hon. members know, western Canada has been dogged by the fact that the area is a single or limited product economy. The diversification which is being built into western Canada's economy by reason of the exploitation of by-products has not only increased employment but also lessened the effects of certain other economic vicissitudes, such as a decline in the market value of some grains, problems of drought in the agriculture industry, and so on. Those adverse factors will not have the same impact they would have had 25 or 30 years ago.
Some reference has been made to the question of foreign ownership, and particularly to the question of whether or not the common stock of this particular company will be made available to Canadians. I think this is a question to which the committee will be interested in having some answers. I should like to make reference to

the fact, as the hon. member for York North (Mr. Addison) has pointed out, that the company is being proposed for incorporation by Pacific Petroleums, a name that will be well known to many members of this house in connection with activities in the Canadian oil industry. The parent company, as the hon. member has pointed out, is one of the last of what unfortunately appears to be a diminishing breed in Canada, the independent oil company. So many of the major companies are now engaged in the business. However, it is a company in which there is a substantial proportion of stock available for acquisition by Canadian shareholders. The incorporation of this particular company, Mr. Speaker, will add another arrow to the quiver of possibilities available to the parent company, and therefore another area in which Canadians will have some opportunity to invest their funds. This is the kind of opportunity this government has been attempting to stimulate in Canada by various taxation measures. It is for this reason I feel this parliament should give serious consideration to the incorporation of this particular company, which would make possible the construction at an early date of the particular products pipe line in question, make it possible for the industries that will be dependant upon the pipe line to develop, make it possible for the products to be produced by those industries and for the pipe line itself to produce income, and particularly to produce Canadian dollars to ease the balance of payments situation which has become so pervasive in our discussions not only in recent years but since the war.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend to the house the approval of this particular measure, and I should like to commend to the hon. member for York North the suggestions made with regard to bringing items of information to the members of the committee, so that the committee may satisfy itself on these particular points and may report favourably upon this bill, which it seems to me will produce great economic benefits to all Canadians.

He said: The sole purpose of Bill S-41 is to authorize the petitioner, Developpement Central Ville de l'lsle Inc., which is a company incorporated under the Quebec companies act, to construct a bridge and causeway over the St. Lawrence river to connect two islands lying off the east end of the island of Montreal near the city of Pointe-aux-Trembles. The nearest island called Ile-aux-Asperges is about 500 feet off shore and the water between is navigable for very small river craft such as small motor boats. Ile-aux-Asperges will then be connected to Isle Ste-Therese by means of a short causeway crossing a very shallow stretch of water. Ordinarily, the only approval that would be required for a bridge

Private Bills
of this sort would be by way of an order in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Public Works. However, because the bridge is over part of the St. Lawrence river, the approval of parliament is required. The bill, however, contains the usual safeguards, namely that the governor in council must approve the plans and location, and that the company must observe such regulations for the security of navigation as may be prescribed by the governor in council. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in presenting to the committee the 1963-64 estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare it should be remembered that this is a department which spends the second greatest amount of public money, being superseded only by the department of my good friend and colleague the Minister of National Defence. I believe that his expenditures represent some 24 per cent of the federal budget, as opposed to about 19 per cent for this department. I feel certain that the Minister of National Defence would be as happy as I to see the day when we can both offer this committee and the country a drastic cut-back in our estimates, if perhaps for somewhat different reasons. In the case of defence spending, I am sure all Canadians would be glad to see world tensions relax to a point where our military requirements would be less demanding, and I am equally sure we would all like to see Canada's economy boom once more to the point where the welfare needs of our people might also be diminished.
I think it will already be clear to all hon. members that these two objectives, the reduction of world tension and the expansion of our national economy, continue to hold the highest priority in the government's thinking and planning. As far as our nation's health is concerned, we will of course continue to spend whatever is necessary to assure Canadians the highest possible standards of health. May I assure the committee that there will be no skimping in this area. The

Supply-Health and Welfare blue book shows that the estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare for the fiscal year 1963-64 amount to $1,204,910,550, or an increase over the last year of $104,908,300, or 9.5 per cent. This is roughly a normal annual increase due to the natural population growth and other reasonably constant factors. However, these figures do not include an additional amount of $3,500,000 made available to the department last year by way of supplementary estimate. That was mainly for the general health grants and hospital construction grants programs. The total amount that I have mentioned, this year as last year, excludes provision for payments under the Old Age Security Act. Until 1962-63 such payments were included within the department's estimates but were classified as a non-budgetary expenditure. As a result of the recommendation of the public accounts committee, however, the department was instructed to delete this item from the main estimates and has done so.
As usual, by far the largest part of the department's budget is earmarked for statutory outlays. These add up to approximately $1,105,700,000, or 91.8 per cent of the total vote. They include $542,900,000 for family allowances, $385,000,000 for federal contributions to hospital insurance, $110,000,000 for unemployment assistance, $38,700,000 for old age assistance-this, of course, is separate and apart from the old age security payments -$19,250,000 for disabled persons allowances, $5,000,000 for payments under the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act, and $4,870,000 for blind persons allowances. The remaining 8.2 per cent, or approximately $99,200,000, represents items to be voted by parliament. It may be that hon. members would appreciate having a breakdown in general terms, and that $99,200,000 is to be spent in the following way: $31 million for payments to the provinces under the general health grants, $20 million for payments to the provinces under the hospital construction grants, $30,063,000 for medical services-which includes provision for Indian and northern health, quarantine, immigration medical, sick mariners, civil service health and civil aviation medicine programs-$2,890,000 for administration of the Family Allowances and Old Age Security Acts, $2,610,000 for our laboratory and advisory services, and $3,459,000 for administration of the Food and Drugs Act, the Proprietary or Patent Medicines Act and the Narcotic Control Act. I might point out here, Mr. Chairman, that the figure of $4,438,000 shown in the bue book as the increase in the voted items actually excludes the $3,500,000 made available as a supplementary

estimate late last year. That, of course, means that the real increase is only $938,000, instead of $4,438,000, in this year's estimates over those of last year.
Two significant items contribute to this increase. One is the provision for the food and drugs directorate of an additional $653,000, more than half of which is designed to cover the first phase of a three year program to strengthen and expand the directorate. The second is the fact that provision for the first full year's operation of the welfare grants program has been increased to $500,000 from $250,000.
The estimates show an increase of $100,470,000 in statutory expenditures, which relate largely to higher federal contributions under two specific programs. The first is an increase of $60 million in the hospital insurance and diagnostic services program, where rising hospital costs, the growing number of hospital beds and greater bed utilization have all inflated the costs. The second is in unemployment assistance, where the development of this program results in an increase of $21,750,000 in the printed estimates. The increase in the provision for old age assistance, blind persons allowances and disabled persons allowances programs, totalling $11,820,000, results mainly from the revision of these three acts. The increase in family allowance payments of $6,900,000 results from the normal growth in the population of those under 16 years of age.
The committee is aware, of course, Mr. Chairman, that a $10 increase was recently voted in our old age security payments. The present forecast of an increase of $71,200,000 in old age security payments comprises $56,700,000 resulting from this $10 increase, which began last month, and the remaining $14,500,000 from the normal increase in the population of people over 70 years of age.
These expenditures by no means represent the total effort and scope of operations of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Indeed, as many hon. members know, we have been stepping up our activities in a number of directions. Much preparation has already been carried out in connection with the Canada pension plan and, as the house is aware, it remains our firm intention to introduce the necessary legislation as soon as possible. When this measure becomes law, it will give this country one of the finest social welfare programs available anywhere in the world.

I might add that the Canada pension plan will be, as many hon. members already know, placed on the agenda of the forthcoming federal-provincial conference on November 25 and 26. As far as this department is concerned, Mr. Chairman, those will be a busy two days. Simultaneously with the federal-provincial conference we will be holding another conference on the reported connection between cigarette smoking and lung cancer.
The hon. member for New Westminster sent me notice of a question about this earlier today, and I might inform the committee now that we are hoping this meeting will provide for an exchange of viewpoints between many of the groups concerned and will reveal those areas in which co-operative action might be taken to ensure a co-operative and effective program.
The participating departments or agencies will include provincial departments of health and, in some cases, provincial departments of education; also represented will be a number of professional and voluntary organizations, such as the Canadian Medical Association, Association des Medecins de Langue Francaise du Canada, Canadian Public Health Association, National Cancer Institute of Canada, Canadian Cancer Society, and the Canadian Heart Foundation.
Tobacco growers and industry will be represented by the Ontario flue cured tobacco growers marketing board, the burley tobacco marketing association of Ontario, office des producteurs de tabac jaune du Quebec, and the Canadian tobacco manufacturing industry. In addition to my own department we will have representatives from the Department of Agriculture. All told, we are counting on 60 delegates to the conference.
As many hon. members are aware-indeed, questions on the matter have been posed to me in the last few weeks-the government is also currently reviewing with the provinces the question of old age assistance payments, disability allowances and blind persons allowances. As hon. members already know, this will be an item on the agenda of the federal-provincial conference to be held in a week or so, and it will be discussed as part of the item with a number of cost-sharing programs.
In the area of food and drug control, Mr. Chairman, a matter which has received even 28902-5-303
Supply-Health and Welfare greater attention in the last year owing to the distressing thalidomide matter, we have already taken action to implement recommendations relating to the introduction of new drugs, and to the tightening of quality control by the manufacturer. New regulations covering these areas were put into effect quite recently, and the staff of the food and drug directorate has been strengthened accordingly.
One other program to which we are paying special attention in view of public interest is that of radiation protection. Authorization has recently been given for the establishment of an advisory committee drawn from universities and other private agencies to sit with our own experts and assist them in the supervision of our radiation protection program. I might add that the division concerned will be moving to a new and specially constructed building on February 1 next. My department is eagerly awaiting the report of the royal commission on health services. Our latest information is that it should be available toward the end of the year, and I am sure all hon. members look forward to an opportunity to peruse this study. All in all, with the funds available to the department as outlined in these estimates, I feel that we will be in a good position to achieve our one basic objective-to make Canada an even healthier, happier and more secure country in which to live.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I begin by mentioning that the former minister of health and welfare, the hon. member for Perth, is unavoidably absent at this moment owing to a previous commitment; hence my beginning the debate on behalf of our party. However, he will be here within the hour.
May I at the outset express my personal good wishes on the floor of this house, although I have expressed them privately to the minister, for her very good health during her tenure of office. I will not elaborate on that, but I do wish her well and hope she has much personal satisfaction and a sense of achievement from her very heavy schedule. There is a general desire among the members of our party to facilitate the passing of estimates generally, particularly these estimates tonight. Therefore, I will endeavour to express only a broad interest in all aspects of the department's efforts, and also to avoid the very obvious controversial aspects of some of the problems facing us in the future. I will endeavour to keep my comments on the estimates for the year 1963-64 to a minimum and as concise as possible.
We in this country happily enjoy the second highest standard of living in the world, which brings with it peculiar and particular

Supply-Health and Welfare problems, problems peculiar to a country adjoining another country with ten times the population. The question is asked on all sides how our services are paid for. This places a very heavy responsibility of leadership upon any government, a very heavy responsibility on Canadian citizens in their requests and desire for services. The Minister of Finance has warned us that unless the national budget is moved toward balance Canada will find itself on the rocks. This is a comment which is well made, but it is easier made in opposition than in government. I wish to express my great sympathy for the Minister of Finance, considering the staggering job he has to do. Businessmen are constantly criticizing government, and I presume they will continue to do so for incurring expenditure which, they fear, will cripple the economy. We must pay regard to such criticism, if we are to maintain the respect of businessmen, who, after all, must face the problems of heavy world competition, and if we are to maintain the respect of the Canadian citizens whose money we are spending.
We must keep uppermost in our minds means by which measures necessary for our national health and welfare can be taken simply and economically. Such an approach has been adopted by many people over the years, particularly by the able staff of the department of health and welfare. When I was connected with the department I noticed how generously and unselfishly the staff worked to meet sudden and unexpected demands on their time and energies. I think it is up to members of this house to meet the social problems which confront us in the same spirit, when it comes to the working out of social policies. We know that the attention we give to health and welfare problems affects our daily lives and personal happiness to a large extent, since it is closely connected with social order and social harmony in our country. I am sure that no one inside or outside this house has any quarrel with the theory of hospital insurance. It is needed, useful and right. But the justice of its administration is something which must be watched carefully and constantly. According to the estimates of 1959-60 the cost of hospital insurance was about $150 million. This year's estimates show the cost to be $285 million, an increase over last year as the hon. lady has stated, of more than $60 million. We realize that to some extent the increase was inevitable due to an increase in the number of hospitals and in the number of people using and staffing the hospitals. In 1958 we almost doubled the amount of federal assistance given to hospital building, alterations and renovations. No one could quarrel with this step, having regard to the improvement in the health of Canadians

and in our society generally which has resulted; but from my own observations and from comments made by doctors it seems to me there is an area of outpatient assistance where the service might have been strengthened. One hears of many cases where patients, particularly chronic and elderly patients, go to hospital because their families for one reason or another cannot afford to keep them at home, though they would wish to do so if it were possible. It may be that a relatively slight increase in expenditure on public health nurses who could visit such cases would be helpful in meeting the needs of patients of this kind.
Undoubtedly, many ideas could be obtained as a result of concentrated efforts, working in co-operation with hospital boards, doctors and all groups interested in the care of the sick. I urge the minister to encourage a continuance of grants by which assistance is given to research into social problems, and to the training of essential workers in this field. It seems to me it would be penny wise and pound foolish to go on indefinitely increasing the already high cost of the care of the sick if we did not pay equal attention to research into cure of disease. Not only should we pay the closest attention to research in our own country but we should improve our communications with other countries and with organizations such as the World Health Organization, so as to be able to take the best advantage of all the work which is being done outside Canada in this field. I feel that in an age of greatly increased research this is one way in which we may be able to reap benefits and eventually avoid the skyrocketing costs of illnesses which we do not yet know how to cure. Along the same lines, I would urge the minister to continue to pay attention to the fitness and amateur sports program, in which I am personally much interested and which, I believe, has a direct relationship with what I have just said about the necessity of research into illnesses and diseases. Both lead towards the goal we should all like to see attained. Both constitute a definite and positive approach to health problems in Canada.
In an effort to avoid repetition I have tried not to deal with particular aspects of the work of the department which will be considered intelligently and constructively by other members of this party.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this seems to be ladies' day in the House of Commons. The hon. member for Winnipeg South was the first member to get the floor when we met this afternoon and thus far tonight the ladies have had all the say.

It is a pleasure to have an opportunity to take part once again in the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I noted the interesting remarks with which the minister began her speech. She pointed out that the Department of National Health and Welfare is the second largest department of government in terms of the amount of money provided for it. The hon. lady indicated that 19 per cent of the federal budget is appropriated to the Department of National Health and Welfare. I think it is profitable to reflect on this for a moment, and to remind ourselves that the word "health" did not appear even once in the British North America Act of 1867. The word "hospitalization" appeared a few times, but the word health not at all. The fact that we now have a Department of National Health and Welfare, with a budget the size of the one before us, indicates the degree of social change that has taken place in the century during which this country has been in existence, as it indicates the importance of the tasks which are the responsibility of the present minister.
I noted too the minister's expression of hope that the sums of money required by the two largest spending departments might in due course be pruned somewhat. She said that the reasons for seeking to cut down the expenditures of the Department of National Defence and the Department of National Health and Welfare were different. I agree with her that the moneys we are spending on defence we hope one day to be able to cut back, and I agree with her there are some kinds of expenditures that are appropriated for her department that we hope we can cut back, expenditures such as unemployment assistance which could be cut back if we had full employment, expenditures perchance on pensions for disabled and other conditions if by programs of positive medical research, such as those just referred to by the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas, we could improve the health of our people. But I think it would be both an illusion and a mistake to suggest that welfare payments generally should be pruned.
I suppose this is a matter of definition, a matter of semantics, and I am sure if the minister and I discussed it a little more fully we would find ourselves in agreement. If by welfare payments one means payments to overcome needs that should be avoided or corrected, yes, we hope the need for such payments can be reduced. But if by welfare payments one means such programs as old age security and the Canada pension plan, which I was glad to hear confirmed again tonight and applauded on the Liberal side of the house, if by welfare payments one 28902-5-303!
Supply-Health and Welfare means money spent on health care, hospitalization, medical research, let us not anticipate these expenditures being pruned. Let us accept it as a responsibility of our kind of society to do more of this kind of thing on a civilized, on a social, basis. In those terms I should like to amend the minister's statement by saying that I hope the estimates of the Department of National Defence can be pruned so that she, or rather her department, whoever the minister may be, can have more of that money in the not too distant future.
I think it is good that both the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas have drawn attention, even in their brief speeches tonight, to the broad range of interests and responsibilities of the minister's department. It not only has the responsibility for pension programs and for hospitalization and health insurance measures, on which I intend to spend most of my time, but it deals with such matters as the control over foods and drugs, research and so on. Another brand new item that not only was not thought about when the British North America Act was drafted but was not thought about not very many decades ago is the question of protection against radiation. These references that have been made both by the minister and by the previous speaker indicate, as I say, the broad range of responsibilities of this department, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare is quite justified in a feeling of pride that it is her honour to preside over such an important department.
So far as this party is concerned, though we share with other members a desire to deal with the estimates of all departments as expeditiously as we can, we do feel we are dealing again tonight with one of the most important services to our people provided by the government of Canada, in co-operation with the governments of the provinces and at other levels, and we think it is a constructive use of our time to have a thorough discussion of the various aspects of this department. The previous speaker indicated that other members of her party would be dealing with some of the specific subjects and the same is true for members of our party. Other members who will follow me will be dealing with matters of research, mental health and various other aspects concerning which we think there should be a tremendous increase of activity on the part of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I should like to speak for a few moments now on the so-called welfare section of the work of the department. The department is, as we all know, divided into two general divisions with two deputy ministers, one a deputy minister of welfare and the other a

Supply-Health and Welfare deputy minister of health. The programs that come under the welfare branch of the department have already been alluded to tonight, old age security, old age assistance, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act, the Family Allowances Act, unemployment assistance and so on. These are programs, of course, that the fathers of confederation never dreamed of. Some people look at them in terms of their huge cost to the Canadian taxpayers. We think it is a mark of growth and a mark of maturity in a country like ours that we have reached the point where we do go in for these transfer payments, or whatever you may want to call them, where we do have this co-operative effort as a people to provide for the security and the needs of our people.
We think that one of the best jobs that the Canadian parliament has done for the Canadian people in the last few decades has been to develop programs of old age pensions, old age security, old age assistance and all the other programs we now have. But, Mr. Chairman, the fact that we have got these programs should not leave us feeling that there is nothing more to do. Every one of the programs now on the statute books, every one of the programs now in effect, needs improvement.
I am going to leave the question of old age security and its companion piece, the Canada pension plan, to the end of this group of programs about which I want to say a few words, and mention the others. Old age assistance, the program under which a pension of up to $65 a month with a means test is paid on a 50-50 basis by the provinces and the federal government, obviously needs improvement right away. I know the minister's answer will be that this is going to be discussed at the forthcoming two day federal-provincial conference, and it certainly is going to be a very busy two day period. Frankly, I think all the other departments should stay away from the conference. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare needs the whole two days herself with the provincial representatives, once she starts dealing with these things.
Take old age assistance, to begin with. Many people in Canada today, even though they are able to understand the federal nature of our government and the difference between provincial responsibilities and federal responsibilities, cannot understand why the pension is now $75 a month for those 70 years of age and over but only $65 a month for those between the ages of 65 and 69. I know that to make that change means that one has to make all the other changes as well. I know this puts an extra burden on the provinces, and that one has to consider all of the welfare responsibilities of the provinces; but I plead with

the minister to take all the time she can get out of those two days with the provinces, so that decisions can be made at the conference and so that progress can be made on these matters without interminable delay.
The same is true of the pension for the blind. It is still at the $65 figure. This pension, as we all know, is paid 75 per cent by Ottawa and 25 per cent by the provinces. Here again, those who are receiving the pension cannot understand why it has not been raised above the $65 figure the way it has for those 70 years of age and over. The same is true of those on the disabled persons allowance. In referring to it, I want to mention also that this is one of the programs which needs a particular review. I have in mind especially the definition of total disability and the list of requirements that are in the act and in the regulations in order to qualify for this pension.
There are a number of people, as all of us know, who by ordinary standards seem to be totally disabled, seem to be unable to work, but who are denied this pension. Sometimes it is because they can feed themselves, which is about all they can do. It is incredible that they should be denied the pension. I run into cases where the man of the family is disabled and unable to work. He still is a man; he still feels he would like to be doing something that would contribute towards the upbringing of his family. The wife has to go out to work because the disabled persons allowance, by itself, would not provide sufficient income. She makes enough that the means test comes into play and he cannot draw any portion of the disabled persons allowance. This cuts two ways. On the one hand, he does not get the money needed to help bring up the family and, on the other hand, he is also hurt in his spirit because he feels he is becoming nothing but a dependant on his wife.
I am raising problems here to which there may not be an immediate solution. But I suggest there are human angles to this legislation as well as financial angles, which call for the legislation to be reviewed. It was a good day in parliament, and I remember it very well, when after years of pressing for it we got a disabled persons act. It was a good day when we got all these other programs. However, let us not think that because we have them, because the administration is handling them in a routine way, all the problems are solved. All of these programs need to be reviewed. Later on in this debate tonight, other members will mention other programs.
Then, there is the family allowance program. I know that others who will take part in this debate will have plenty to say about

that. It is quite a long time since the amounts paid by way of family allowance were fixed, and they have never been changed in any real sense from the beginning in 1945. Today we have only two levels of payment rather than four, as was the case at the start. In any event, the maximum amount of the family allowance has not been changed since the act first came into effect on July 1, 1945. There have been many promises across the years to increase the amount of the family allowance. There have been many promises in recent years, particularly by the party now in power, to extend the family allowance beyond the age of 16 for those who are still in school. As yet, we have seen no sign of anything of this nature.
I trust I have said enough in respect of these various programs that come under the welfare branch of the department to substantiate my suggestion that they need to be reviewed. I recognize the state of federal-provincial relations in this country. I recognize the virtue of co-operative federalism to which the Minister of National Health and Welfare made reference the other day. This is an expression which I think, so far as political parties in this country are concerned, was first given currency by this party in the program we adopted at our founding convention in 1961. I am glad to see that it is now in such general use. But let us not allow the need to consult result in interminable delay. Consult not for two days but for two weeks, and keep at it. Let us get these various programs sorted out, so that some of the feelings of injustice, some of the sufferings our people are enduring, are overcome.
I have left to the last of the items coming under the welfare branch of the department the joint question of old age security and the Canada pension plan. From now on, there is no question but that these two items are companion pieces; these two programs go together. Our movement started supporting some years ago a two-stage pension plan. We called for an improving of the universal pension by bringing it to the higher amount it is now, $75, and building on top of that a contributory pension plan for all our people. I say quite frankly that we were delighted when the Liberals started talking in language similar to ours. We were pleased when the Liberal party made a promise to the electorate in 1962 and 1963 that a two-stage pension plan such as we had advocated would be brought into effect. I need not at this time repeat the remarks I made on October 29 during the grievance period at the end of a supply debate to which the minister responded. I simply remind the committee that we think we are reflecting the views of the country generally when we express our regret
Supply-Health and Welfare that the plan that was promised so specifically in the election campaign, promised so precisely in the speech from the throne, is to be delayed.
I call upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare to work as hard as she possibly can to sell this plan to her own cabinet colleagues, to sell this plan to the provincial governments with whom she will be meeting on November 25 and 26. I call upon her to launch various programs of education, if she will, to sell the idea of the Canada pension plan. I think it can be sold to the Canadian people. I think it is disgraceful, and I might use a stronger word, the job against the Canada pension plan that has been done by the insurance companies and other vested interests. I noted what the minister said on October 29, that the government is not free to spend public money to try to answer that program. However, the government has 125, more or less, Liberals over there. They are not very busy in the House of Commons. I am sure they are looking for something to do. They support the Canada pension plan. Every time one calls for its inauguration, every time the minister says it is still coming in, they applaud. Why not give them material, give them information on the plan, and give them the job of selling to the country the virtues and values to all the Canadian people of the kind of pension arrangements that are envisaged in the Canada pension plan.
If the minister is prepared to accept suggestions from me, I suggest she might put something in the hands of all members of parliament. I think the Liberals would be glad to do this job. I think every member of parliament would. I am not too sure, when I hear the complaints about the Canada pension plan that have come from members to my right, where that group stands. However, I believe even they could be sold on the idea. If the minister wants a specific suggestion, I remind her that a long time ago, before she ever thought of coming to parliament-as a matter of fact on July 29, 1944-there was laid on the table of the House of Commons a draft bill respecting health insurance, public health, conservation of health and prevention of disease. I am going to refer to this when I get to the health section of my remarks, but I mention it now in relation to pensions. At that point the government of that day was promising it was going to do something about health insurance in the immediate post-war period. It found a way-the record shows it and I could explain it to the minister-to lay on the table of the house a draft bill with no resolution ahead of it, no first reading, and no debate at all.
The draft bill was tabled, printed and widely circulated. As a matter of fact Liberal

4752	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare candidates used it extensively during the 1945 election campaign as an indication of what they would do; but my point in raising this is that I think the minister could find a way to lay on the table of the house a draft bill of the Canada pension plan. There can be the safeguarding kind of note that makes it clear this is not the final form, that it is subject to change after consultation with the provinces and after reviewing various facts, but I think it would be a help to the job of education if she did so, or if some such piece of literature were made available.
The white paper that she tabled on July 18 was an excellent document, but I have run into people who do not see it that way. They do not think it explains things in detail. I am satisfied it does, but if in addition to the white paper we could have a draft bill or some such document for the public to see it would be an awfully good idea.
There are other things to be done. The minister's speech, or at least the speech made on her behalf on September 30 in Toronto, was an excellent reply to the critics of the Canada pension plan. This is something which is not only the possession of the Liberal party and the present government, but it is also the possession of the parliament of Canada and the Canadian people. Let us have the objections brought out in the open, and if changes need to be made let us make them. But let us not lose the plan. Let us not have it go down the drain for want of our people knowing or understanding it, while its opponents, who have a vested interest, have a heyday in their fight against it.
I suggest that the minister consider presenting a draft bill, or referring the subject matter to a committee. In fact I think a tremendous job could be done by hon. members in selling this idea, and to do this at this stage I suggest would be extremely valuable.
As I indicated, Mr. Chairman, the Department of National Health and Welfare has its two main branches. I have spent my time thus far talking about the welfare branch, but there are the two branches, each being presided over by a deputy minister. As a matter of fact the hon. member for Winnipeg North, who will be following me a little later, will speak about one particular aspect of the health branch, but the one point I want to emphasize now is that we think the time has come for health insurance or medicare in this country.
I know that the Liberals get a little tired of my reminding them that sickness insurance, which was the language used then, was promised in those two words, plain as could be, by the Liberals in 1919. In 1944 this draft bill I have been talking about was laid on

the table of the house, and it is included in the Journals of that session for July 29, 1944. There were also two or three reports about that time, huge documents, and all kinds of work was done on it.
The proposals were then laid before the federal-provincial conference of 1945, and across the years this idea has been held before the Canadian people. Meantime, of course, we get the propaganda of those interested in private insurance, that most people are covered. I thought Pierre Berton answered that very well in a recent article entitled "The Big Lie About Medicare Insurance", which made it clear that those who have some kind of medical insurance do not constitute 70 per cent of the total, as private insurance people claim, but that only 50 per cent have any kind of insurance, and something of the order of only 18 per cent have health insurance that is really worth anything in time of ill health or medical crisis of any kind.
These things add up to the urgent need in our time for a medicare or health insurance program, and there is no question but that the best way in which to have such a program in this country is similar to the hospital insurance legislation, for the federal government to pay a certain percentage of the cost-we think it should be a rather high percentage-leaving the administration of the program to the provinces.
If Quebec seeks some particular arrangement for itself, we think the government of Canada should be prepared to agree to that particular arrangement; but our plea is that the government not rest on its oars because it has got hospitalization on the statute books but that it move on in this very important field of medicare and health insurance. It took nearly 40 years from the first promise of sickness insurance in 1919 to get the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act on the statute books.
The Liberals got that act on the statute books, but it did not come into effect until they went out of office. I remember when they were in office and gave us this act we felt it suffered a deficiency in that it did not include tuberculosis and mental illness. Then the Liberals came across to this side of the house and tried to get the Tories, who succeeded them, to put into the act what they themselves did not want to put in it; and now they are back on the other side of the house again, but they are silent on these points.
This is another piece of legislation that needs to be improved. It all adds up to these two things, that the legislation we have in this field, whether it is on the welfare side or the health side, needs review and needs to

be improved. This goes lor all of the welfare programs and for the hospitalization and health programs. But, over and above the need for improving these things, we need early action on the Canada pension plan and medicare or national health insurance.
We know these things are costly and we know there are difficulties today, in the light of federal-provincial relations, in sorting these things out; but surely we Canadians are not people who are stalled in our tracks because things are difficult or costly. If they are worth while we can find a way; we can effect the necessary co-operation.
We think that these things that will bring a better day in terms of the security and the health of our people are worth while, and I call upon the minister and the government to give parliament and Canada a lead so that we can get on with these important programs.

Mr. Chairman, if there are estimates which are hard to criticize, it is truly those of the Department of National Health and Welfare. When the house is in supply, members of the opposition usually claim that the expenses are too high in certain fields and they try to make suggestions.
Since I have not yet heard such remarks, I would say that the opposition parties want the government to spend more in some respects. As far as I am concerned, if I had any suggestion to make, I would spontaneously mention family allowances, a topic which has already been dealt with by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
Now, I feel that the most important question the minister will have to consider is that of assistance to large families. Indeed, she probably would just have to spend a short while with the Minister of Finance to have part of the revenue from the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials transferred to the heads of families who are out of work because construction has slowed down in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I must say that I somewhat sympathize with the Minister of National Health and Welfare whose political impartiality is well known, since she is now at the head of a department where she has to keep nearly all her party's election promises and try to please everybody.
I believe that it is customary to make, on behalf of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the most attractive promises during the election campaign. I feel therefore sorry for the minister, Mr. Chairman.
This afternoon, I was looking at the British North America Act. I think the minister
Supply-Health and Welfare would do well to look up subsection 16 of section 29. She would find that her only responsibility, according to the constitution, would be as "Minister of the Quarantine", since at that time, this was about the only power allotted to the federal government in the field of national health and welfare. That would probably relieve the minister, and during her leisure hours she could go on with her studies of constitutional law, diplomacy section.
Mr. Chairman, I must direct my remarks also to the Minister of Finance since, although it is up to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to fulfil election promises, it is up to the Minister of Finance to foot the bill.
I think the problem we have to face is a harrowing one for both ministers. The best example we have in this respect is the pension plan, which has been promised, which we have been and are still waiting for and which we shall be waiting for, for a long time to come.
That is why I say to the minister that if she really wants to make her department a success, she should go back to the constitution and look after "quarantine", and this is just a preamble to my remarks on her estimates.
I considered the estimates which have been presented and I found that at least ten and even 12 joint programs are mentioned, plans for a federal contribution to certain provinces, including the province of Quebec and several other provinces, in the welfare field.
This gives me an opportunity to express my opinion on a word everyone uses now and which used to make the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre happy; he said it was coined by his party and marked the beginning of a new era, the era of a new federalism. All parties and all provinces talk of the new federalism.
The other day I was listening with some interest to the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) when he dealt briefly with this aspect of the question. The hon. member for Three Rivers has been criticized in certain places and congratulated in others. But it is the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who drew my attention to this, when he introduced a motion to censure the government's attitude concerning federal-provincial relations. And when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle blamed the federal government for bringing in measures that came under provincial jurisdiction without consulting the provinces, I must admit that he was right.
Because we heard again this evening accusations which are often levelled in the house at the Conservative party who, allegedly, has done nothing during the six

Supply-Health and Welfare years it was at the helm, I feel I must praise the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) and the Conservative party for their action in the fields of federal-provincial relations, of bilingualism, and biculturalism; they have certainly achieved more in six years for the province of Quebec than Louis St. Laurent when he was in power. I have to admit it. It is true that when the Conservative party was in power, it tried to complete the work left undone, while from various sides one heard cries of "too little and too late". It was not really too little or too late, though it might have seemed to be too little because patience was wearing thin.
Quebec had waited a long time for action. I must give its due credit to the Conservative party, who has really tried, and opened the door to the improvements that are brought in today by the party in power. Quebec was looking towards the Liberal party, and waiting hopefully for a solution. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle is quite right on that point.
Since it came to power, the present government has only brought down two or three pieces of legislation, and even so it has been compelled to beat a hasty retreat at the last moment. If Messrs. Daniel Johnson and Rene Levesque had not intervened, the newcomers of the Liberal party, set against any centralizing measure, would have been overcome by the old guard, who were hardened centralizers.
Does all this mean that on this matter, the present Prime Minister, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) are insincere? No, I do not think so. But after listening during several weeks to speeches in this house, after listening to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said recently, I thought to myself that what is wrong, is that the very concept of confederation is out of true. We got to a point where the Prime Minister only has to invite over a representative from each of the provinces of the country and tell them: "Now, I am going to interfere with your jurisdiction, if you see no objection." If those representatives say they have no objection, everything is legalized and becomes constitutional. And we are expected to believe that the principle is safe. To take all the trouble of gathering the representatives of the ten provinces around the conference table, just to ask for their permission to legislate. To my mind, that is the great weakness of our present system.
I did not want to engage in a discussion on confederation versus federation, but as the estimates before us give me a chance and as we have prominent professors of political science in the house who do not want to do so, I shall try to explain why those concepts are all wrong. I think that a true confederation is a union of ten independent provinces pursuing a common aim.
A federation, or the new federalism which is so much discussed, is a different thing. It means a group of states or provinces gathered around a central mandatory government.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased that the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare gives me the opportunity to discuss the social legislation in general that this department administers.
In the last 30 years, the house has agreed to pass various social measures to help those Canadians who found themselves in a less favourable situation than their fellow citizens as a whole.
In fact, legislation to help children, families, old people, the disabled and the blind was enacted. And although those measures were meant to help those people, when the time came to implement them, they were found to contain provisions that made it impossible to attain the objectives we had in mind. That is precisely the point on which I want to call the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh). She should certainly consider my suggestions if she wants to help the government set right certain injustices.
Our legislation concerning old age security and old age assistance are examples of this.
Under those two pieces of legislation, if the head of a family has reached the age where he is entitled to the old age pension but his wife has not reached that age, both he and his wife have to live on a pension which was established for one person only. This kind of situation is not normal and should be set right. In my opinion, the Minister of National Health and Welfare should bring in an amendment to enable both spouses to get a pension even if the wife is ten years younger than her husband.
Both the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act should be amended along those lines.
Let us move on to the Disabled Persons Act. A short while ago, the hon. member for

Supply-Health and Welfare Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated that, for the purpose of the act, the definition of total disability is very strict.
In fact, as mayor of the town of Beaupre, I was asked to study the case of certain disabled persons and to help them get a pension. That is how I came to realize that serious injustices were done because the definition of the word "disability" is much too strict. In that connection, allow me to speak of a man who had both legs and one hand amputated because they had been frostbitten. In fact, he had only three fingers left on the other hand. I tried to get a pension for that man and when I was turned down I had to tell them: Are you going to wait until he has his head cut off?
This is an anomaly that should be corrected at all costs in order to make this act more humane and to see that it serves the purpose for which it was enacted.
There is also another provision under this act that should not be applied. It is paragraph G-2, subsection 2, of section 3. This section provides that a disabled person is not entitled to a pension when husband and wife earn $1,980. It is utterly inhuman to oblige two persons to live on $1,980, more especially when one of them is disabled.
As far as the Blind Persons Act is concerned, the situation is somewhat different, in that two people are allowed to earn $2,460.
Now, what happens when a family head is disabled or blind? Because she wants to give a little more comfort to her family, to her children, in short, enable them to live as well or almost as well as their neighbours, the mother goes to work in order to earn a few dollars. When that happens, the officials of the department reduce the pension of the blind or disabled person, and that because these people have shown energy and courage in trying to improve their lot. They penalize them. They say to them: If you work too hard, if you earn too much money, we shall reduce your pension.
That is another anomaly which I suggest the minister should correct immediately.
Mr. Chairman, I come now to the Family Allowances Act.
During the last electoral campaign, supported in this by nearly all the other political parties, the Liberal party promised to increase family allowances and to extend them to age 18. As for us, we had asked that they be extended up to age 21.
Well, at the beginning of the present session, we suggested that family allowances should be increased and we even submitted a notice of motion to that effect. I should

like to say that the comments we have received on that score have been, on the whole, rather favourable.
On June 17, 1963, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) said, as can be seen on page 1251 of Hansard:
Our party is committed to extending family allowances to children at school to the age of 18 years. At the appropriate time, I am sure this legislation will be brought before this house to implement the commitment which was firmly made during the course of the election campaign. However, I presume one of the purposes of this measure would be to extend family allowances and make them the basis of a salary for students attending university.
The hon. member carried on for a little while, as if he were not satisfied that we would thus be reminded that we had brought pressure to bear on the government since the beginning of the session in order to obtain an increase in family allowances.
On July 3, when the house was still dealing with family allowances, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) said, as reported on page 1806 of Hansard for that day:
I conclude by saying that we have a policy on family allowances. We did mention it during the election campaign, and the program will be fully carried out but give us a chance to catch our breath. We must be given sufficient time to see what should he done. If that is not enough, do not forget that we did much more in 60 days-
Mr. Chairman, four months have gone by since the Minister of Justice asked us to give a breathing spell to the government. They must surely have caught their breath since then and they should be able today to increase family allowances, for if we fail to do so, we seriously wrong our Canadian families and our Canadian children. Since the beginning of this session, we have voted millions of dollars for large firms and municipalities, in short, we have voted millions for this and that.
I am in favour of these things, to improve markets, promote the economy. Our party supports all that.
But we also know that there are no better means of activating the economy than to increase the purchasing power of families all over Canada, because if it is distributed all over this country, it will promote the national economy and at the same time we shall solve a part of the unemployment problem by activating consumption which, in turn, will activate production.
I think it would be the most just and human means to activate the economy of this country.
Consequently, in view of the excellent steps taken by the government until now and in order to do justice to Canadian children, I move with the support of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):

That the Minister of National Health and Welfare should, in the opinion of this house, consider the advisability of increasing family allowances as soon as possible.

Resolved that a sum not exceeding... be granted to Her Majesty for... for the year ending 31st March, 1964.
That is the only resolution which is before us.

I was reading from the end of citation 238 which appears on page 201 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. Now I would ask members to look at citation 242 on page 203. The first paragraph is a lengthy one. Let me read the last part of it:
Each resolution for a grant forms a distinct motion which can only be dealt with by being agreed to. reduced, negatived, superseded or withdrawn. The committee may reduce the amount of a grant by the omission or reduction of the items of expenditure of which the grant is composed. Here the power of the committee ceases.
Subparagraph 2 says:
The only motion allowed, when a resolution is under consideration in committee of supply, is that the amount be reduced or that the chairman leave the chair (either without making a report or to report progress on certain resolutions).
Subparagraph 3 states:
Each resolution can only be dealt with by being agreed to, reduced, negatived, superseded or, by leave, withdrawn, and the withdrawal can be made although the decision of the committee has been taken upon amendments proposed to the resolution.
Then, once again, follow the words:
Here, the power of the committee ceases.
Another sentence in the same paragraph states:
It is not allowable to attach a condition or an expression of opinion to a vote or to change the destination of a grant.
I think the point is quite clear, Mr. Chairman. I am all in favour of my friends in the
Supply-Health and Welfare corner trying to get the government to implement its promise to increase family allowances. I urge my friends to make all the speeches they want about the matter and to move their amendments at the proper time, but I plead with them to recognize the clearly established procedures in committee of supply. There are many other opportunities to move substantive amendments, but when we are in committee of supply we do not have the opportunity to move these expressions of opinion.
I make this as a contribution to the point of order debate, but I also make it as an appeal to my friends in the corner not to treat this as the kind of thing to appeal and to put the house in the ridiculous position of appearing to vote on the subject of family allowances, when we would not be doing that. What is before us now is the established and proper procedure of dealing with money votes, and the only thing we can do is vote for the item, vote against it or reduce it. We cannot change its destination; neither can we attach a condition to the vote. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it is clear that the proposed amendment is out of order; but I hope that, even as you permitted me to speak on it, you will hear others who may wish to speak before you make your ruling.

I think that if the minister and her colleagues would pay a little more attention to the manner in which they answer questions they would be more consistent in their replies than they were in this case.
While I compliment the northern health services and the expanded facilities in general, I must say that when it pertains to dentistry it is a different story. I think a great deal of improvement could be made in the dental health services in the north. I might give just one instance. There is a lack of dentists in a great many of these northern areas and it falls upon the R.C.M.P., the missionaries and other people in these areas to extract teeth in an emergency. I am thinking in particular of one missionary at the Hollow Water reserve whose father was a missionary before him. This man undertook this role and has performed it up to this time. Now the Department of National Health and Welfare has cut off the supply of local anaesthetic to this missionary. When dealing with this matter I may be treading on rather precarious professional ground, but I must implore the minister-and I wish she would listen when I am imploring her-to do something in this regard. I would tell the minister that it is not very much fun having teeth extracted without anaesthetic, and if I need to prove that assertion to her or any of her officials, I would be only too glad to do so. I would


implore her to reinstate the practice of supplying this missionary with local anaesthetic so that in the case of an emergency he may make an extraction and will not have to do so without anaesthetic.
Also in my riding we have the model town of Pinawa. A $600,000 hospital will be constructed there shortly. In this regard I might say that when the Conservative government came into power in 1958 we increased the federal health grant from $1,000 to $2,000 per bed. I think it is time the department reconsidered these grants, especially in view of the action taken by this government in imposing a tax on building materials, to see whether they should not be increased further. I think other speakers will have more to say about this matter. I wholeheartedly agree with the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas who said the increase in the cost of the hospitalization program is alarming. I think several things could be done by the department to perhaps curb this expenditure. I am not going into detail on this question because I am sure other hon. members will deal with it.
Previous speakers mentioned family allowances. I am wholeheartedly in favour of the principle of extending family allowances beyond the age of 16 years to those children attending school. I certainly hope the present government will not do what it did with the increase in the old age pension in 1957, when they implemented it just before an election and left the succeeding government to pay for it. I hope they will bring this about, and bring it about soon. I would like to say a few words about the old age assistance, and pensions to blind and disabled persons. I think the government is certainly not following the good example set by the former government, which increased the old age assistance and the pensions to blind and disabled persons simultaneously with the increase in the universal old age pension. I am at a loss to understand why the department has not taken similar action. We said we were willing to pay the increase if the provinces would agree to do their share and implement this program. We have been talking about federal-provincial conferences and everything else in this house as if this were some new principle that was being introduced. As far as I am concerned, the government is offering no leadership whatsoever in this regard. These are the very people who need this increase most, because they are being paid these pensions on the basis of need. I can only conclude that the government is trying to mark time and put this matter off as long as possible in order to reduce somewhat the record deficit which they are going to have.

These are a few suggestions on general matters that I wanted to place before the minister. Now, as a member of the dental profession, I would like to say something about the role dentistry plays in the community and what part the federal government should play in extending dental services more universally. The people of Canada spend about $125 million a year on dental services. This represents 8 per cent or 10 per cent of the amount of money spent by the Canadian public on health services. I think that is a quite significant fact. It will be more significant, I think, when I say that of the national health grants only 1 per cent is allocated to the field of dentistry and dental health. I think it is incumbent upon the government to at least raise this amount to the level of the percentage of money spent by the people on dental health services as compared to the health dollar in general. I think this percentage should be raised to 10 per cent. That is certainly not out of line. The niggardly amount of money that is being spent on dental research is illustrated when we see that only 15 cents is spent on dental research for every $100 that is spent on dental treatment. I know that a certain amount of money is being provided by the federal government to be spent through the national research council. I think the grant is something in the order of $200,000. This amount should be substantially increased. I am taking the liberty of quoting these figures to show the importance of dentistry to the community as a whole. I might say that I feel the staff in the dental division should be increased. I understood they have provision for three full-time dentists in the dental division. There is one vacancy there now. I hope that vacancy will soon be filled and that as soon as possible the staff is substantially increased. I am not criticizing the members of the dental division because X think they are dedicated, optimistic, and are trying to do a very good job with very limited financial support and encouragement from the department. But I think more and more emphasis must be placed on this field. As I say, that can be done through increased dental health grants toward dental research. I know the staff have on the boards a large number of very vital research projects, such as research into oral cancer and research into the etiology of periodontal disease. When we think that one out of every two teeth lost is lost because of periodontal involvement, then these developments are very important.
I place particular emphasis on research because dental diseases are almost universal. At the same time it is sad to think they are almost universal, because they are also
Supply-Health and Welfare largely preventive. It is in the interests of our economy that the federal government should encourage research and preventive and educational measures in order to cut down substantially on the incidence of dental disease and on the amount of money which needs to be spent by the public and by the government on dental treatment.
I think emphasis on dental education of the public has to be placed on proper oral hygiene and proper diet, because preventive measures can largely eradicate a large number of dental diseases which lead only to disastrous and expensive complications. When we consider that only one quarter of the population receive any regular dental treatment it is understandable that education will do a great deal to bring this number up.
One of the preventive measures we can encourage and emphasize is fluoridation. I mentioned fluoridation once before in the house and I got all sorts of letters from all sorts of people, and even all sorts of threats. However, this is a measure I commend to the people of Canada as a whole and to the government in particular. Studies across Canada show that five out of every ten of our four-year-old children and eight out of ten of our six-year-old children have suffered from dental decay, and that the average child when beginning school has five decayed teeth. This is quite a sad commentary on the state of dental health in Canada. In the town of Stratford, where they have natural fluoridation, the incidence of dental decay in the same age group is about one quarter of what it is in the population as a whole. I think this would show that fluoridation of community water supplies is a very important and economical preventive measure in dentistry.
Let me say that the cost of fluoridating a community water supply runs about 20 cents per capita per year. In other words, the cost of a single filling will fluoridate the water supply for a person for 20 to 30 years. All sorts of studies on millions of people have shown that fluoridation of water supplies will cut down the incidence of dental decay in children by two thirds, and this general dental health is carried on into adulthood. Surely we can see the millions of dollars which will be saved by the public in general if we adopt fluoridation more widely. It is being adopted more widely across this country now, but I hope it will be adopted even more widely when we compare the 20 cents which it might cost to fluoridate a community water supply per person per year with the average expenditure of over $20 per person on dental treatment.
I should also like to speak about health insurance in its relationship to the dental profession, and the attitude of this profession

Supply-Health and Welfare towards health insurance. I should also like to make some remarks with regard to the implementation of dental health insurance in conjunction with the universal form of contributory or other medical health insurance. I think the Canadian Dental Association should be commended for its very broadminded approach to this subject. They have come out in favour of a dental health insurance program. They have done a great deal to study the problem, but the problems which face dental health insurance are far more serious than those which face medical health insurance. A relatively predetermined amount of people every year have to undergo medical treatment. However, it is recognized that almost everyone has to undergo dental treatment, and it is therefore very difficult to apply general insurance principles to universal dental coverage.
The dental association is very cognizant of this fact and is very careful in laying down the ground rules under which dental health insurance can be brought forward. They say that they are willing to co-operate with the government but that there are certain principles which they would like to see recognized. For example, the principle of freedom of the patient to choose his dentist; the freedom of the dentist to choose his patient; a system of remuneration which is mutually acceptable and preferably based on a fee-for-service basis. There has to be co-operation between the patient, the dentist and the government. The people who are chosen to administer this program should be people who are approved by the profession, and the public, and they should not serve strictly a political function.
There are various methods of introducing a program of this sort. The first one is that the government must bear some responsibility before introducing such a program for doing something to provide assistance to educational institutions and to provide the personnel necessary to carry out this program. That is one of the first things the government must recognize.
This is, of course, largely a provincial matter. However, I think that if the federal government is going to impose a system of compulsory dental health care universally it must recognize that it has a role to play in educating the personnel. Second, it must recognize that through education of the public a large amount of dental treatment can be avoided. Therefore, a great deal of emphasis has to be placed on public dental health education, and a lot of it at the federal level. The third matter is that if a comprehensive dental health program is introduced there is obviously going to be the necessity for auxiliaries because of the shortage of dental manpower, and very careful steps must be taken


in this program to institute a training scheme for these auxiliaries.
There are two principles which could be brought to bear in the introduction of a dental health program. First of all, you might as well wipe out of your mind the idea that everyone can be covered at the beginning. There are only two ways in which a dental health program can be attached to a general health insurance program. The first of these would be by introducing the lower age levels or school age levels, and then advancing the plan to include the general public. Second, they could adopt some such plan as now exists in Manitoba. Here the service is provided for those who are indigent, in receipt of mothers' allowances, and so on. These all have medicare cards. They present them to their dentists and are entitled to free dentures and other services as required. The dental association itself administers this plan. It is paid a per capita fee by the provincial government to cover expenditures, but the administration, as I have said, is carried on by the association itself. We prefer this because it is less complicated than filling out endless forms in duplicate, triplicate and quadruplicate as has to be done now in dealings with the Indian affairs branch, the Department of Veterans Affairs and so on. If we do not adopt one or the other of these approaches a situation will be created in which the best interests of dental health will not be served.
In Manitoba the dental association recognized its social responsibility by agreeing to accept a lower rate of remuneration for the work done for these indigent patients. It realizes that it must do something for those in the community who could not otherwise be looked after. I think the program in Manitoba works very well, and it may be one way of introducing a program on the national level. More idealistic people feel, of course, that eventually everyone should be covered. I agree with that view, and I think the dental association would agree with it. However, we must avoid the pitfalls. Let no one think it is possible to sit behind a desk and figure out that people will get dental coverage on the same basis as medical coverage, because the dental field defies insurance principles. If an attempt is made to cover all Canadians, premiums will be so high as to be prohibitive.
At the present time, dental associations are studying prepaid dental plans. Pilot projects are being instituted, but even on this basis they are running into all kinds of difficulties actuarially. For this reason I want to emphasize the need for proceeding with due regard for the difficulties of the situation. I believe the dental profession in Canada should

be complimented for its public spirited attitude towards the need to extend dental care services in Canada. I think they are trying to play a role commensurate with the ideal of rendering the best dental service possible to the people of Canada. I believe that with the co-operation of the government such a service could be extended universally. I look forward to that day and I can assure the government that it will get the wholehearted co-operation of the dental profession.
At the same time, I should like to see steps taken immediately in the fields of education and prevention to see that the groundwork is laid for the day when this plan can be realized. I hope it will not be brought about merely as a measure of political expediency as has happened recently in a province, causing turmoil and friction between the profession and the community. I hope we shall never see that happen in Canada at large, and that the experience in Saskatchewan will teach us that that was the wrong way to go about it.

speechtext: Any health service you have in Manitoba you got from Saskatchewan.
