I do not think the hon. member should complain too much, because he was run out of that province as a whole, for what he did in Saskatchewan.
I commend to the minister the suggestions I have made and I hope she will sink her teeth into them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking to these estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Springfield upon the constructive suggestions he has made. It was an interesting speech and I am sure it will be of benefit to the country as a whole. In the course of his remarks he made a comment to the same effect as one which the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas had made previously, namely that the expenditures under the heading of health and welfare were mounting so rapidly as to be worthy of careful scrutiny.
I wish to comment on this very theme, because the cost of health and welfare in this country is rising at such a rate as to place many of the provincial prepaid hospital schemes and medical plans in serious jeopardy. The cost of hospital care is rising like a meteor in the sky. In the estimates themselves it will be seen on page 264 that the statutory payments for hospital services, including assistance to the provinces under those agreements, in the current year ending March 31, 1964, have increased by $60 million from $325 million to $385 million. That is an increase of almost 20 per cent in one year.
When the prepaid hospital plan was first introduced it was announced in no uncertain
Supply-Health and Welfare terms that this was to be a three way partnership. We were told, and many of us believed it for some years, that it was to be a three way partnership between the provinces, the individual premium payers and the federal government. We were told that this partnership would work in harness like a troika, or three abreast. After a few years of interesting work in the field of health, I find the troika is still in harness but that it is operating as a tandem now, with the provincial department of health in the lead, the premium payer in the centre and the federal department of health and welfare bringing up the rear. The second and third partners in the team have to take the pace from the leader.
I am certain that many of the expenditures being made today by the provinces under the heading of health with the co-operation of the federal government could have a lot of the fat trimmed from them, and I should like to make two or three suggestions which I believe are worthy of consideration. Indeed, consideration must be given to them, since costs are mounting day by day. First of all, let me say I found it a pleasure to stand shoulder to shoulder with the Minister of National Health and Welfare in her work. She has her heart in her department and she gives it the closest of attention. She took part in the provincial election campaign in Ontario eight weeks ago, and I was happy to stand with her at that time on the questions of the day. The committee may recall that the hon. lady emphasized the fact that the Canada pension plan could be introduced without funding. That is a straight statement of fact: It can be done. It would not require funding because the government, having the power to tax, is in a position to keep the plan in operation without its being funded. But I draw attention to the situation in the province of Ontario, a situation which, no doubt, is being duplicated in the other nine provinces. It was only in January, 1960, that the hospitals of Ontario instituted a pension plan for their employees. Previously, individual hospitals had not been able to offer a pension plan because they could not afford its cost. Those who held employment in hospitals either had to look forward to working until they died or had to hope that the small insurance policy they were paying for 100 per cent themselves would carry them in their old age.
But on January 1, 1960, a pension plan was instituted among the hospitals of Ontario under the Ontario hospital services commission. There is an interesting thing to be found in the first two annual reports of the hospitals of Ontario pension plan. There have only been two annual reports so far. The first report covered a period of 18 months from January 1, 1960 to June 30, 1961 and the
476S

Supply-Health and Welfare second report covered the period of a year from July 1, 1961 to June 30, 1962.
The interesting thing about the reports is the fact that when the pension plan was introduced on January 1, 1960 a large number of employees of Ontario hospitals went on pension immediately, although there was no funding of the pension plan at that time. They had completed the necessary years of service and had attained such an age that they were eligible for pension. But in the second report for the year ended June 30, 1962, an amazing statement is made by the auditing firm that audits the pension plan. It is pointed out in the second annual report that the hospitals of Ontario are paying into the pension plan the astounding sum of $3,400,683 a year.
In an editorial last Friday with reference to the need for more nurses the Ottawa Citizen makes the statement that when the Ontario government introduced its hospital insurance plan it acquired a vested interest in the province's hospitals. That, of course, is a straight statement of fact. The hospitals have no individual autonomy today under the Ontario hospital services commission. As a hospital man from Port Arthur stated, individual hospitals are free to do anything they are told. I mention this so that hon. members will understand how much the government, through the department of health, dominates the work of the hospitals in the province.
When the hospitals of Ontario are paying $3,400,000 per year into the pension plan compared with a contribution by the employees of $2,255,000, then I put my finger on what I can only describe as an unnecessary expense. The pension plan of the hospitals is the responsibility of the Ontario government. The Ontario government through its department of health should collect from its hospital employees but it should not be paying $3,400,000 a year into that pension plan.
In a paragraph in the second report it is interesting to find a statement by the pension committee of the hospitals of Ontario pension plan, which committee, of course, is being advised by insurance executives and insurance agents. With respect to the year ended June 30, 1962, they say:
Past service costs of the plan were amortized over a 30 year period and this unfunded amount will require annual payments of $539,785 over the remaining 28 years.
There is no requirement whatsoever that this pension plan be funded. It is a government responsibility, and to state that we must have a funded pension plan when the government is behind it is ridiculous. If the government should go bankrupt, all pension plans in the provinces would fall by the wayside, and this extra expense is absolutely unjustified. That sum of over half a million

dollars a year for the next 28 years will amount to $15,113,980, and bear in mind that the federal government is paying approximately one third of the cost of this more than half a million dollars into a fund that is not required at all.
I also hold in my hand the annual statement issued by the hospitals of Ontario pensions plan to a hospital employee of some years standing. It is interesting to note that on the back it says:
The hospitals-
That means the government.
-pay the entire cost of past service pensions.
Under the Old Age Assistance Act, whose payments the public calls pensions but are properly described as old age assistance, there is no funded plan to make sure that the payments of $75 a month are made to the elderly, and if we have no great fund behind the old age assistance plan why do we have to go to the expense of building up a fund behind hospital pension plans throughout the Dominion of Canada?
I am very happy that the minister has brought in her estimates before the federal-provincial conference in two weeks time, because I do believe this is one subject that should be taken up with the provinces. It should be pointed out to them that some of the expenses should be carefully scrutinized, because some of them are unnecessary.
Another point to which I should like to refer has to do with a question I asked the government to advise how much money had been allocated year by year to hospitals throughout Canada by way of grants toward nursing. If hon. members will look at page 263 of the printed estimates they will find midway down the page a reference to the fact that the federal government pays $750 per bed for living quarters for nurses. I would point out that nursing is the only profession, the only career, the only form of employment in which the candidate for education has to be given residence accommodation. If a girl wishes to be a lawyer she has to look after her own residence accommodation. If a girl wishes to be an architect she has to look after her own residence accommodation. If she wants to be a veterinarian she looks after her own residence accommodation. If she wants to be an artist she looks after her own residence accommodation. But if she wants to be a nurse the provinces go into a tizzy and build palatial residences at a cost to the taxpayers that in my estimation is unnecessary.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member is forgetting that while the nurse is taking her training

she also works about eight hours a day for nothing, or possibly $6 or $8 a month.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a point I intended to mention this afternoon in discussing the resolution respecting technical and vocational training assistance and which I intend to refer to on Monday when the bill comes before the house. I believe that girls who decide to train as nurses should be paid by the hour for the work they do, and with the money in their purses they can then look after their own accommodation. I do not believe that in the year 1963 we should have indentured labour being paid on the basis of board, lodging and uniforms.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Your hospital costs would really go up then.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I was referring to the cost of residences for nurses. We have this great Department of National Health and Welfare, and I believe it was the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas who mentioned that it is the second largest spending department of the government. When one considers some of the demands that people make on it, he wonders how long it will be before the department becomes the largest spending department of the government unless there is careful scrutiny of the requests that are made.
I presume that in no place in all of Canada is there more uproar today over the shortage of hospital beds than in my own city of Toronto which now has a demand before the federal government for millions of dollars for necessary hospital construction. To my mind, to spend millions of dollars at this time on a calculated shortage of 2,360 hospital beds in Toronto when we have been having annual deficits nationally of between $500 million and $700 million a year would be ridiculous. At the present time there are in the city of Toronto 1,791 beds for student nurses scattered among 23 hospitals in the city. I can see no reason why the bed accommodation in these residences for nurses, who are young and most active and vigorous, should not be made available for hospital bed accommodation to meet the shortage of hospital beds in the area at this time. There is a calculated shortage of 2,360 beds, with 1,791 beds being used by active young nurses in training. These figures would indicate that the nurses are getting better treatment than the patients who are sick, injured and dying because we are told that hospitals are refusing entrance to patients since the hospitals claim there are no beds. The administration of the expenditures under the co-operative scheme between the provinces and the federal government, could certainly stand close scrutiny for the benefit of the taxpayers of the Dominion of Canada.
Supply-Health and Welfare
There is another angle to which I should like to draw the attention of the committee and the Department of National Health and Welfare, and that is connected with nursing education. Many hospitals operate schools of nursing. Why is this so? It is the only field of education that does not fall under the departments of education of the ten provinces. If doctors can be educated under the direction of the department of education, if dentists can be educated under the direction of the department of education, why cannot nurses be educated under the direction of the department of education? There is an expenditure involved in educating nurses. Most hospitals will tell you that there is a cost to them for educating student nurses, even when consideration is given to the services that they perform now for penurious remuneration. But if the education of nurses were to be placed under the department of education in all ten provinces, where it properly belongs, then the cost to the departments of health in the ten provinces would be reduced and the money that the federal department of health allocates to hospital work would not need to be squandered on nursing education under the guise of health grants. These payments could be diverted 100 per cent to health services.
The interesting feature here is the fact that only last Sunday the largest hospital in my riding, Humber Memorial Hospital, Weston, held open house for its new addition. It now has approximately 360 beds, and opened up four extra floors last Sunday with about 500 people going through the corridors examining this greatly improved institution. The hospital authorities gave the visitors small booklets describing the work of the hospital. One of the paragraphs in the booklet points out that the hospital is going to build a school for nurses, which will be the first school for nurses in Ontario not requiring residential accommodation. This morning I spoke to an unimpeachable source at Queen's Park, Toronto, by telephone and asked if the requirement that a hospital desiring to operate a school of nursing must have residential accommodation had been withdrawn. I was advised, no, the requirement has not yet been withdrawn from the hospital regulations of the province.
I was told, too, that Humber Memorial would not be the first to have a school for nurses without a residence because another hospital, which was not named, had made application to institute a system of training nurses without having hospital beds provided for them. This indicates that there are at least two hospitals in Ontario that realize it is not necessary to spend money on nurses' residences in order to educate nurses in our

Supply-Health and Welfare province to the degree of registered nurse. I believe that if the federal authorities would state they were going to withdraw this grant of $750 per bed for living quarters for nursing students, they would establish a precedent that would be followed all across the Dominion of Canada. We would find the present residential accommodation turned into hospital beds for the sick, and the young girls who wished to be nurses would seek their own residential accommodation the same as other students do.
Now, I am talking about the fat that can be removed from these expenses.

speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. A few minutes ago the hon. member for York-Humber made a statement about money being squandered on nursing education. I am sure that he really does not mean that. Could he please explain what he means by that statement?
Also, I should like to point out to him that the nursing profession is Canada's oldest profession. There is a plaque out in the hall honouring Jeanne Mance, a nurse, the first professional person to come to Canada in the seventeenth century, and I am sure the hon. member does not mean those words.

speechtext:
I have but one more point to make. When I first rose to make my remarks, I stated that I agreed 100 per cent with the hon. member for Springfield and the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas that there must be corners in which the expenditures made by the Department of National Health and Welfare could be reduced, if careful attention were paid to the money that is being spent. I should like to refer to one small matter, perhaps, but right now the hospitals in the province of Ontario are engaged in a study of insurance against malpractice suits. This insurance is taken out by all hospitals in order to protect them against any suits that may be instituted by patients, their relatives or friends, who may claim that the hospital technique was faulty and sue for malpractice. We have been investigating this question of malpractice insurance for the past 14 months, and within the next four or
[Mr. Cowan.l
five months I am sure a very interesting statement will be made by the Ontario hospital association on that matter. Let us stop to consider the question of expense.
In the November issue of the Canadian Doctor, there is a long article in which the author points out that, in his opinion, hospitals should increase the amount of malpractice insurance they carry. This makes me wonder why the hospitals should pay the premiums for malpractice insurance. As it is now, the hospitals are paying the premiums but the hospitals do not perform the operation. The doctors are not the employees of the hospitals; they are individual practitioners. This is an expense that is saddled on the hospitals today, and this is something that could be investigated to the profit of the taxpayers of Canada.
I should like to say that I only make these suggestions because I believe there is fat in the estimates that could be cut out. As I said before, we are running in tandem, we are not running in troika. I sincerely hope the minister will bring up these matters at the provincial conference in two weeks time for the benefit of every Canadian taxpayer from coast to coast.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in these estimates the government proposes to spend almost $500 million for the health needs of the people of Canada. The major part of this amount of money is to be spent-and we in this group certainly have no objection to this -in the provision of grants to the provinces

Supply-Health and Welfare toward the hospital plans which have been enacted. Yet one would have to look at the estimates with a microscope to find the amount of money spent by the federal government in the field of mental health. This is, to say the least, an amazing fact when we realize that half the hospital beds in Canada are now occupied by people who are mentally or emotionally ill. More than 70,000 people are receiving treatment in Canadian hospitals for mental or emotional illnesses. Twenty five thousand new cases are admitted every year.
This government has failed to realize that one in every 16 Canadians born today will spend part of his or her life in a mental hospital. The government seems to have failed to realize that people in mental hospitals are not stupid; they are not defective; they have received the same education as the rest of us and until they became ill they were able to work and support themselves and their families. Of course, the minister will deny that the government has a defeatist attitude in this regard, but one has only to look at the expenditure for hospitals to realize this is a fact. We are today spending over $23 a day to keep a person in a general hospital, while we are spending $5.90 a day to keep a person in a mental hospital. Why this disparity? I suggest the main reason for this disparity is the decision of the former Liberal government when it instituted the hospital plan, continued by the Conservative government, and decided to keep mental hospitals out of that plan. The result is that we are spending this very small amount of money in mental hospitals.
What does this mean to the patient? I want to read a very few paragraphs from a report which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of May 28, 1960. This report is over three years old, but not much has happened in the province of Manitoba in the field of mental health since then. Indeed, not much has happened in any other province since then. I would remind members of the committee that the Winnipeg Tribune is a Conservative newspaper. It was describing the program in the province of Manitoba under a Conservative government. I did not think it intended to exaggerate; in fact I am certain it did not exaggerate. Yet what do they say:
Rigorous austerity, idleness and lack of rehabilitation facilities highlight the tragic conditions endured by some 3,000 mental patients in Manitoba.
These men and women of a forgotten cause are crowding the wards of six mental hospitals in this province-and get less recognition than criminals in the penitentiary.
Lord knows, that is bad enough. Then they say:

Unwanted and unknown, they wait in apathy for recognition that will bring their standard of treatment and accommodation at least level with those existing in federal prisons.
Further, they say:
Patients who could be rehabilitated if given proper treatment remain on in their drab wards indefinitely and usually develop a second mental disturbance called ''desocialization and degradation", a man-made condition resulting from loss of hope.
Of Manitoba's six mental hospitals, two are overcrowded, three are full and have waiting lists and only one operates with a slim margin of empty beds.
The article continues:
Brandon mental hospital has a total of 1,622 patients and a bed capacity for 1,317.
This hospital has a staff of two certified psychiatrists and one psychiatrist who is about to receive certification. It has no trained social workers and no rehabilitation facilities.
Selkirk mental hospital has been forced to stretch its facilities to the limit. It has a capacity for 1,005 patients and houses 1,245. It is also seriously handicapped by shortage of staff, old buildings, overcrowding and no adequate rehabilitation program.
It has a staff of three certified psychiatrists and one experienced psychiatrist. Like Brandon, it has no trained social workers.
It is no wonder that the people who become mentally ill and who are forced, because there are no better facilities, to enter one of the provincial mental hospitals, stay there for months and years longer than they ought, when you compare the program of activities and the rate of recovery in the provincial mental hospitals with the rate of recovery in the psychiatric wards, small as they are, in the general hospitals. There is a fantastic difference in this respect. But this is not surprising when you realize that the psychiatric wings in the general hospitals, which consist of 50, 60 or 20 beds, usually have as many as or more psychiatrists at work than there are in the provincial mental hospitals. This is not criticism of the provincial mental hospitals. In every province they have increased their expenditures in this regard at a great rate; but they are meeting the same kind of cost problems in this as in other fields. They have said, in fact that there is nothing more they can do at this time.
Tremendous progress has been made in this field. The vast majority of patients can get well. But they will not get well, or they certainly will not get well as quickly as they could, if we do not do more than we have done up to this time. The first step we ought to take is include mental hospital costs in the payment of hospital grants by the federal government, or at least the same share of mental hospital costs as we now pay in regard to other hospital services. I suggest that we will not meet the costs and problems of mental illness by building more hospital beds,

because that is what we have been doing essentially. We are not going to meet this problem until we are prepared to take the lead in getting more people, more psychiatrists, more psychologists, more psychiatric nurses and more of the other technical facilities and people needed to work in this field. We will not do that until the federal government is prepared to take the lead, in co-operation with the provinces, in extending the program of training psychiatrists.
The Canadian psychiatric association in its brief to the royal commission on health estimated that we need to double in the next ten years the number of psychiatrists we are training in our training institutions. In Canada in 1961 we had one psychiatrist for every
30.000	people, while in the United States they had in the same year one psychiatrist for every 14,000 people. In Soviet Russia they had one psychiatrist for every 12,000 people, and in Great Britain they had one psychiatrist for every 20,000 people. To reach by 1970 a ratio of one psychiatrist for every
15.000	people, which would still be less than these other countries had in 1961, we would have to double the number of specialists in psychiatry. The cost of training this number of psychiatrists has been estimated by the Canadian psychiatric association to be $4 million a year. To attain this end, of course, we will have to do more than just provide training grants; we will have to provide a much larger number of teachers at the university level and in the hospitals. The Canadian psychiatric association has estimated that this will cost $1 million a year for university training purposes. Similar expansion is needed in the field of clinical psychologists and psychiatric social workers, occupational therapists, and so on, and this only the federal government can do. I suggest that if the basic problem of mental illness is not tackled, costs will rise to an astronomical level and tens of millions of dollars in the coming year will be spent merely to keep people in hospital. These are people who could be out of hospital if we did the job which needs to be done.
One of our biggest lacks in recent years is in the field of research on mental illness. In 1961 the United States government spent $48 million on mental health research. In the same year in Canada we spent on a per capita basis 16 per cent of that spent by the United States. Last year we spent just over $700,000. It seems to me the height of foolishness to spend this piddling amount to deal with what is the greatest unsolved medical problem in the country. Yet the medical profession over the years has recommended that we get down to the problem.
In 1957 the former Conservative government appointed a committee to review the 28902-5-304
Supply-Health and Welfare question of support for medical research by the government of Canada. This committee made a report which was tabled on November 12, 1959. I will not deal with it in detail but I should like to read some of the conclusions leached by this expert committee. The minister will find this on page 32 of the report:
The present level of support falls far short of requirements. The most obvious inadequacies are as follows:-
(a)	Grants: Many important projects are not supported because of lack of funds and others are restricted to only a fraction of their full development.
(b)	Fellowships: Present stipends of research fellowships are too low. More fellowships are required.
(c)	Scientific personnel: The Canadian medical schools lack the funds to employ an adequate research staff.
(d)	Fluid research funds: There is a need for fluid research funds in the medical schools, to be administered by the deans.
(e)	Research facilities: Research space is inadequate in all medical schools; in many cases this is the most serious restriction on research development.
This report dealt with the conduct of more medical research, but the lack of research facilities is particularly noticeable in the field of mental health. Yesterday the Governor General opened a new research centre in the field of mental health in the city of Montreal. This is a tremendous institute and it was a great day for the Dominion of Canada. But I point out to hon. members that this is the only research institute in the field of mental health of its kind in the country. If we are to get the people to work in this field and begin to attack the problem at its roots, then we will have to do much more than we have.
Mention has been made of the cost of mental health to the people of the country. The direct cost has been estimated by the Canadian psychiatric association for the year 1960 at $239 million: $149 million has been spent by the provincial governments in their mental institutions; $10.5 million by the federal government in grants in aid to the Department of Veterans Affairs and other departments, such as justice; $14 million in psychiatric beds in general hospitals; $2.5 roughly in psychiatric beds in private hospitals; and $63 million in medical care paid to medical practitioners and for medication. But the Canadian psychiatric association has calculated that the indirect cost of mental illness in 1960 was $626 million: $100 million for the loss of average manpower earnings by resident patients in hospitals, and $526 million for the loss of earnings of patients in industry due to mental illness and emotional disturbance. So, Mr. Chairman, we can see what a tremendous and fantastic problem we have to face. I should like to think that in the next ten years the federal government will do ten times as much as it has in the last ten, because even with

Supply-Health and Welfare that amount of money we would only begin to touch the fringes of the problem.
Comment has been made about spending too much money. We are spending a great deal of money every day and every week in the field of health and welfare, but no money could be better spent because we are losing fantastic amounts of money in private treatment, and by people who can ill afford it, because the governments of Canada, both federal and provincial, have not really faced up to their responsibility.
In my constituency a few years ago, before the institution of a national hospital plan, one man was in the position where his wife was ill and he was advised to send her to another province for the particular kind of assistance she required. The cost of keeping her in hospital ran to some $200 a week and she was in hospital for four months. When this man added the cost of the medical bill of the doctor, which was not exorbitant if one thinks in terms of his experience and training, the only way he was able to meet the cost of this particular case of mental illness in his family was to sell the one asset he had, his house.
Another constituent of mine whose wife was ill was a member of the Manitoba medical services, which the doctors of Manitoba, and I think rightly, feel is the best plan of its kind in the Dominion of Canada. Unfortunately, the group to which he belonged was disbanded because it was too small. He was therefore not eligible, because of the decision of the Manitoba medical services, to join as an individual member, so he had to meet the cost himself. His wife was going to a psychiatrist once a week and paying a fair fee, from the point of view of the psychiatrist, of $15 for a one-hour visit. This meant that this man was paying $60 to $70 a month to enable his wife to see the psychiatrist. He had three children in the family and the normal cost of medical service for those three children ran in the neighbourhood of $10 to $15 a month; so you can see from that, Mr. Chairman, that his medical bill ran to around $1,000 a year.
Very few of us can afford that kind of bill. I am not being critical of the doctors; I am simply pointing out the kind of expenses people are forced to pay in the field of mental illness simply because we have not devised a plan which will meet their needs. People plagued with mental illness are able to offset their medical costs by deducting them from their income tax, and this is a step in the right direction. But we have made no provision for a situation where a husband has to hire a housekeeper as the only means of keeping his home going. So the cost of mental

illness in Canada amounts to an astronomic figure. This would be largely unnecessary if Canada were to establish a system of the kind which has been established in some other countries and in certain states of the United States. I disagree completely with hon. members who have said tonight that hospital costs could be reduced. Hospital costs will have to be substantially increased if the federal government is to accept its full share of responsibility and include the same percentage of grants to provinces in respect of mental hospitals as they do now with respect to general hospitals.
I hope the minister will come to the house next year with proposals which will help improve the position of people who are suffering greatly in this field.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I want to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) who was piloting her department's estimates in the house for the first time. I am convinced that she will administer that department well, her love for work and her devotion to duty being well known.
Since there is very little time left, I would like to point out a few facts.
I am happy to note that a very important correction has been made with regard to the province of Quebec in the estimates for the current fiscal year. At page 263 of the estimates, I find that in the field of grants for the building of hospitals, Quebec will get 23 per cent of the total amount this year, compared with 13 per cent in 1962, which means that if there was an injustice in 1962, a timely correction is brought at this time.
Second, I want to point out that the Department of National Health and Welfare is a very important one and the party to which I belong, has always been interested in the activities of that department.
During this session, we have made some improvements within that department. I wish to point out here that we have followed our program and even though some are accusing us of not having implemented it in full, we have already carried out part of it. We have increased by $10 a month, the old age pensions.
In my opinion, it is reasonable to assume that we cannot implement, in one session only, the whole program which we have laid down for the administration of our country, for a period of four years. We intend to carry out the program we outlined to the electorate. We will implement it because we will be in power long enough to do so.

I take this opportunity to ask the minister to give special consideration to the program of allowances for young people of 16 to 18 years of age.
In my opinion, it is increasingly important to introduce such legislation because more and more parents provide an education for their children.
We must help families give a proper education to their children. This piece of social legislation should be introduced as soon as possible to promote education in all the provinces.
I should also like to say a word about amateur sport. I notice that this comes under the minister and that some items of our platform deal with that topic.
I feel that physical education is unsatisfactory at present in Canada. We should have a better physical education program so that our young people would be physically fit for the tasks they will have to face in life.
I submit that the minister should attach particular importance to amateur sport. Although we often spend millions of dollars in other departments, to increase the prestige of our country, we unfortunately find that all amateur sport bodies, at the present time, complain they do not receive enough assistance to develop athletes able to adequately represent our country in the various international competitions. I think a healthy national pride is involved and I consider that the minister should give this point a very special attention.
Frequent reference was made to research during the few contributions to the debates of the house today. I submit to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that research is a very important field since, at the present time, solutions to certain diseases which are constantly spreading should be found. And I believe that should we improve the research situation in that field in granting more credits to research, we could thereby cut down the sums we are presently appropriating for hospitals. I feel that the present department should conduct more thorough studies in that respect.
I would also like to touch on another very important point, which is of tremendous interest to the members of the province of Quebec. It is the pension plan that was submitted to the house and was deferred until a later session. It is essential for the country to establish a pension plan equally favourable to everyone. We must take into account, however, the present requirements in the country. On the other hand, we know that under the British North America Act, social security comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. But through some amendments, it was possible at a certain time to allow the 28902-5-3041
Business of the House
federal government to intervene in that field. I am convinced that the present government acted very wisely in establishing this plan, thus showing to the house that we really intend to carry out our program.
While negotiating with the provinces, we have realized that certain difficulties had arisen, but I am convinced that through negotiations and discussions, we will find an acceptable solution, so that each worker in our country may take advantage of a satisfactory pension plan.
Mr. Chairman, it is now ten thirty. [Text]
Item stands.
Progress reported.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I wonder whether the leader of the house could outline the business for tomorrow, and maybe, for the first part of next week.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I should like to give as complete a picture as possible. I hope there is-and I am inclined to think that there is likely to be-an understanding that, by unanimous consent, on motions tomorrow I would move a motion, for the drafting of which I am indebted to the hon. member for Peace River, which would have the effect of bringing the subjects related to the two bills on the territories before the mines, forests and waters committee next week. I understand this might be agreed to without debate and the two bills would be left on the order paper for consideration after the committee's deliberations have been concluded. I have discussed this with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who is agreeable to having this course taken if there is an understanding that it could be done as a most exceptional and unusual arrangement, really in exception to all rules and only by unanimous consent and only if everyone is genuinely agreed that this is the right way to make progress and that we will do it without debate. It is an exceptional course, but I think everyone feels we have got into a situation that we want to find a way out of. I am not asking for unanimous consent now. I will ask for it tomorrow on motions and if I do not get it we will not be able to do it, of course. I thought it only fair to give notice of it. I have talked to hon. members of all parties and groups opposite but I thought I ought to let everybody know.
When we reach orders of the day tomorrow we will go on from where we left off with the vocational training resolution, which I gather we have practically disposed of. If we can get first reading of that bill we will then

Business of the House
take the bill itself as the first item of business on Monday. If we dispose of this matter the next item tomorrow will be the motion to set up the special railway committee, to be followed by the resolution, No. 14 on today's order paper, regarding the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act. We would hope to dispose of the resolution stage and first reading of the bill. I believe the hon. member for Kingston has had some conversations with hon. gentlemen opposite and there is an understanding that rapid progress could be made with that bill. We would hope it would also be available for Monday after the vocational training bill has been disposed of.
There are some other resolutions we would like to get on with if we could. It will be a long day. These resolutions, of course, are just preceding bills and it is generally better to debate the bills when we at least know what we are talking about. There is No. 15 on today's order paper, the resolution respecting the National Centennial Act which we would like to get through if we could, so that we could have that bill available for the beginning of next week. Then there is a very small matter, No. 19 on today's order paper, an amendment to the Admiralty Act which the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice is prepared to take tomorrow.
Then there are a number of resolutions standing in the name of the Minister of Transport, order No. 16, regarding grade crossings, order No. 17, regarding the St. Lawrence seaway authority and order No. 20 regarding the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation. We would be glad to take any of these we could tomorrow. I may say that
these items would not be called on Monday because the Minister of Transport will not be available, but we would hope to have any of them that are not disposed of tomorrow available again on Tuesday.
On Monday, in addition to the vocational training bill and, I hope, the currency, mint and exchange fund bill and any of these other measures that have advanced sufficiently to be dealt with, if we should run out of business by any chance I believe the Minister of Justice is prepared to have his parliamentary secretary proceed with the amendments to the Bankruptcy Act. Quite frankly, I am not quite optimistic enough to think that it will be reached, but I do not believe any of these matters I have mentioned are contentious at all and it would be quite a display of businesslike activity if we could dispose of all of them. I can assure hon. members that if that should happen before Monday evening there are one or two items on the order paper that could be called to keep the house busy until ten o'clock. The same program would be carried on on Tuesday for all items that have not been finished.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask about the estimates for tomorrow evening?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: As I announced last night, we hope to open the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the government would be very happy if it could be concluded. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will be available to conclude his department as well.
It being twenty two minutes before eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
Friday, November 15, 1963
